Mr. PERLEY moved that the House do on Monday next go into Committee to consider the following resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Canada Grain Act, chapter 27, of the statutes of 1912, and to provide that whenever application is made to the Board of Grain Commissioners for the appointment of an inspecting officer or weighmaster, or both, at a place which is not a terminal point or a regular inspection point, the board, if satisfied that such an arrangement should he made and that the applicant is a responsible person, may order such arrangement as it deems proper, on condition that, besides the fees payable, the excess, if any, of the cost of carrying out such arrangement over the amount of such fees, shall be paid by the applicant in such manner and at such times as the board may determine; and that the provisions as to the inspection and weighing of grain, and as to the appointment of inspectors and weigh-masters, and of any rules and regulations made under the said provisions, shall apply at every place with respect to which such an arrangement has been made; and also that the annual license fee payable by the proprietor, lessee or manager of any terminal elevator, shall be twenty-five dollars; the annual license fee payable by the owner of an eleva-

Mr. W. M. MARTIN (Regina) asked for leave to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the urgent necessity that the investigation of western freight rates now pending before the Railway Commission should be proceeded with at once so that the unjust burden under which the people Mr. PERLEY.
of western Canada are labouring should be removed without delay.
And leave having been granted:
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have no particular apology to offer for bringing this matter before the House at this time. It is a matter which should have been brought before the House and the Government at an earlier date; but owing to the fact that we have had a very prolonged session dealing for the greater part of the time with the Naval Bill, I have not had an opportunity of bringing it to the attention of the House before to-day. This question, as we all know, is of great importance to the people of western Canada. All the representatives in this House from the western provinces know that there is scarcely a question in regard to which more time is devoted in the West or of which more is said than this question of freight rates. It is not my intention to go into details to show that western freight rates are higher than eastern freight rates or to take up time by going into figures. As I said, my main excuse for bringing the matter to the attention of the House at this juncture is the vast importance of the question to the people of western Canada. I have other reasons, one being that statements have been published in certain newspapers to the effect that the Government of Saskatchewan or the Government of Alberta or both have asked their representative before the Railway Commission, Mr. M. K. Cowan, of Toronto, not to facilitate the investigation. I wish to place before the House a statement by Mr. Cowan contained in a newspaper very recently showing that this report is without foundation. I find in the Winnipeg Free Press, of April 18, in a despatch from Ottawa, this .statement:
In order apparently to detract attention from the dallying of 'the Dominion counsel a rumour has been circulated by certain Government members of the House here to the effect that Saskatchewan and Alberta have witliddrawn their counsel from the case. Upon this rumour being brought to the attention of M. IC. Cowan, who was at the capital a few days ago, Mr. Cowan stated that he. had heard of no such rumour, and that there were no reasonable grounds upon .which to base such a rumour so far as Alberta and Saskatchewan were concerned. ' If there is nny such, rumour,^ h© started, it is hbso-lutely false and untrue. The only instructions I have is to pursue the same course in the future as I have done, and that is to do my best to get relief from the burden of unjust freight rates under which Alberta and Saskatchewan are unjustly suffering.'
That I think should dispose of the statement that has been circulated in some newspapers to the effect that Saskatchewan and Alberta were not anxious to proceed with the investigation before the Railway

Commission. Another reason which I have for bringing the matter to the attention of the Government at the present time is that after an examination of some of the records of evidence that has been given before the Railway Commission, I am satisfied that there has been undue delay in the conduct of this investigation. Since April 16, 1912, when the Railway Commission in accordance with the provision contained in section 77 of the Railway Act, and on the ground that Mr. Cowan, acting on behalf of Saskatchewan and Alberta, had made out a case of discrimination in favour of eastern Canada as against western Canada, ruled that it was necessary for the railway companies to justify their freight rates, over a year has elapsed, and nothing has been done by the counsel representing the Dominion Government or by the railway companies. Although two or three meetings have been held since that time, at which evidence was taken, so far as arriving at any result is concerned, practically nothing has been done since April 16, 1912. That is the main reason I have for bringing this matter to the attention of the House to-day.
Without going into details, I believe that the removal of the unjust freight rates in western Canada would to a great extent alleviate the conditions under which the people of that country labour at the present time. We in western Canada know that the past year and the present year up to date, have not been very successful years in that part of the Dominion. I am not here to say that western Canada is not a good country; I believe it is one of the best countries in the world. At the same time the people of western Canada to-day are not enjoying such good conditions as perhaps some men in eastern Canada think, and that is due in part to the unjust freight rates which we have to pay in that country. They are also partially due to the shortage of the crop in 1912. That crop did not turn out to anything like the extent that was anticipated in the early part of the season of last year. The present conditions are also due partially to the shortage of farm labour. Every man who comes from western Canada knows that last year, in particular, it was almost impossible to get farm labour to harvest the crop. It was a very common thing in the district from which I come to pay $4, $4.50 and even $5 a day for an ordinary farm laborer. Another reason is the difficulty of getting grain shipped. I have seen it stated in some newspapers that the conditions which existed in western Canada last year, in regard to the shipment of grain, were better than those which had prevailed in 1911. Owing to the better weather conditions, I believe there was an improvement in the shipment of western grain during 1912-13, as compared with 1911-12, and 1910-11. At the same time I make this
statement, and I can substantiate it by figures, that at every point in Western Canada, outside of the competitive railway points, there was a shortage of cars during the fall of 1912 and the spring of 1913. Another matter which has contributed to the conditions in western Canada to-day is the low price of grain. I speak from personal experience when I say that I have seen wheat that was selling in Ontario for ninety to ninety-five cents per bushel, selling for from fifty to fifty-five cents a bushel in Western Canada. It may be said that the Ontario grade was better than the western grade and I am not in__ a position to compare them, but taking the same grade there was a difference of between forty and forty-five cents in the markets of eastern Canada compared with the price in the markets of western Canada during the past year. Another thing which has contributed to the conditions in western Canada, and this is where the freight rates again come in, is the high prices we pay for every commodity in western Canada. Take the price of cement for instance. In Ontario it was selling for $1.20 per barrel, while in Regina it was $3.25 per barrel, and I am told that the difference of $1.80 was due to the freight rates on the shipments from the East to the West. However, these are not matters with which I intend to deal to-day.
The question which was placed before the Railway Commission in the fall of 1911, was that of discriminating freight rates in the West as compared with the freight rates in eastern Canada, not on shipments coming in or going out, but in regard to the local freight rates in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, as compared with the local freight rates in Ontario and Quebec. In the fall of 1911 or in the early part of 1912 the Railway Commission conducted an investigation into the western freight rates. That investigation was undertaken as the result of many representations which had been made to the Railway Commission by boards of Trade in western Canada, and- also by members of Parliament from western Canada and, I believe, by the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean). As the result of these representations, and having had from one hundred to two hundred complaints presented to them from western Canada, the Railway Commission ordered an investigation into the western freight rates, and the Dominion Government appointed counsel to represent the people of Canada in the investigation. The onus of carrying on that investigation before the Railway Commission rests upon the Dominion Government counsel, and if the Dominion Government counsel are not forcing it in the way they should, in order to get a decision within a reasonable time, the responsibility rests upon this Government. All the Min-

ister of Railways and the Government have to do to-day is to instruct the counsel whom they have employed, and who are the servants of the people, to get the Railway Commission to fix a date when the investigation must go on, for, as affairs stand at the present time, as I shall show from the records of the proceedings before the Railway Commission, no date has been fixed for the resumption of the investigation since January of the present year. A period of four or five months have elapsed since anything was done, and I submit it is the duty of the Dominion Government counsel, who are in charge of this investigation, because the counsel for Saskatchewan and Alberta are not in charge, being there simply by the courtesy of the Railway Commission, to instruct the Dominion counsel to have the investigation completed, and to insist that the railway companies should justify the discriminating rates that exist in western Canada pursuant to the order of the late Mr. Justice Mabee made on April 16, 1912, when he stated that a sufficient case had been made out by the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta to shift the onus on to the railway companies. Up to the present time the railway companies have not justified those rates.
I want to give the House a very short history of what has taken place before the Railway Commission. The first meeting of the commission to investigate those western freight rates was held in the city of Ottawa on February 13, 1912. The meeting was adjourned for a period of one week to enable Mr. H. W. Whitla, of Winnipeg, who had been retained as counsel for the Dominion of Canada, to make demands for information from the various railway companies. That was all that was done on that occasion. On February 20, 1912, the Railway Commission met again, and the session was enlarged again until March 8 to enable counsel for the railways to ascertain what material covered by the demand of Mr. Whitla they would be able to produce, to state to the board what material they could produce, and to formulate their objections to certain of the demands made by Mr. Whitla. I find by the records of the Railway Commission that at this meeting Mr. Whitla represented the Dominion Government, and he had associated with him Mr. Du-Vernet, of Toronto, and Mr. Morrison, of Vegreville. Mr. DuVernet withdrew, and in his place Mr. James Bicknell, of Toronto was appointed. At a meeting of March 18, Mr. James Bicknell and Mr. H. W. Whitla and Mr. F. A. Morrison appeared as counsel for the Dominion Government, and the records also indicate that Mr. M. K. Cowan, of Toronto, appeared as counsel for the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, with the consent of the Rail-Mr. MARTIN (Retina).
way Commission. The case was then adjourned until April 16,	1912, on which
date it was intimated by counsel representing the Dominion Government they would be ready to go on. On March 8, 1912, counsel representing the Dominion Government said they would be able to go on within a period of four or five weeks. The meeting of April 16, 1912, was the most important one that has yet been held by the Railway Commission in connection with this matter. I wish to point out from the records what took place then because it was on that day and subsequent days that the evidence put in by Mr. Cowan, acting for Alberta and Saskatchewan, induced the Railway Commission to make an order that the railway companies must justify the discriminating rates in western Canada. For the purpose of making the record somewhat complete, I refer to whaJt took place on April 16. Mr. Whitla, counsel for the Dominion Government, said at page 4093:
Mr. Whitla: As I say, Mr. Chairman, the productions were only made within the last few days and it may be quite possible that the figures which have been given us and will be given us may have to be checked by competent men before we can accept them as
Hon. Mr. Mabee:	Are you asking for a
further enlargement?
Mr. Whitla:	X may be compelled to but I
would not say that, Mr. Chairman. I have no intimation from the railway companies when I may expect the first production, it may be within the nexit two or three diays. If I can get the further productions I may be ready to go on in a week.
On the 16th of April, the counsel for the Dominion Government were not ready to go on in spite of the fact that they had had three months in which to get the material ready. Mr. Whitla further said that it seemed that the only way in which to proceed was to fix a day so that the matter would not be left wide open. Then Mr. Mabee said: 'We have done that twice now.' Mr. Beatty, solicitor for the Canadian Pacific railway, stated that he had received on the third day of April a statement from Mr. Bicknell of what had been received from them. I quote:
Mr. Beatty states that he received on the 3rd of April a statement from Bicknell of what had been received from them.
Hon. Mr. Mabee: Then that has been in your hands two weeks?
Mr. Whitla:	No, a very small portion of
them. I had copies for perhaps two days before I left Winnipeg but they are so disconnected and they are picked out from all the demands so that we cannot institute any comparison, otherwise I would have been very pleased to have started to-day. Now that is our misfortune but not our fault.
From this statement of Mr. Whitla it is clearly shown that on the 16th of April,
*

1912, Mr. Whitla asserted before the Board of Railway Commissioners, in the presence of all the counsel, that they would have been pleased to have started that day if they had the figures from which they could make the comparison. That state of affairs on the 16th of April, 1912, is interesting, when it appears again on January 7, 1913, that Mr. Whitla and Mr< Bicknell were still not ready to proceed with this investigation. I quote from the record, page 4096:
Hon. Mr. Malbee: This i.s ithe third time we have tried to get this started. How many more times must we come hack?
Mr. Whitla:	That is exactly what I am
anxious to find out.
Mr. Cowan:	I am anxious on behalf of
Alberta and Saskatchewan to proceed. I have some witnesses subpoenaed here to-day and I am prepared to proceed on behalf of these two provinces.
Hon. Mr. Mabee:	Very well, call your
witnesses.
A very peculiar thing took place when Mr. Cowan asked to be allowed to call his witnesses. Objection was then taken by counsel for the railway companies to Mr. Cowan being permitted to put in evidence on behalf of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and the counsel for the railway companies was assisted in that position by Mr. Whitla, counsel for the Dominion Government, who said, amongst other things, at page 4099. This, mark you, Mr. Speaker, is the statement of Mr. Whitla, after the counsel for the railway companies had objected to Mr. Cowan being allowed to proceed:
It is to be considered whether it is advisable to receive evidence at this stage which may possibly be ill digested and not properly prepared for the purpose of an exhaustive investigation of this kind and which may afterwards either be removed from the files or evidence contradictory introduced. I do not know what Mr. Cowan intends to adduce, he has not given us any intimation, but at the same time as I said before, if the commission desires to take evidence now which can only be ' piece meal ' evidence we would welcome any assistance at this stage which the commission sees fit to take.
Hon. Mr. Mabee.- Now it was understood before as I thought that we were to have new evidence submitted to-day to get this inquiry under way and get it started. It was distinctly stated on a former occasion that the commencement of the inquiry need not be delayed until all the information, statistical and the like, had been compiled, but that the inquiry might proceed and we might get along as best we could with the information that came to hand and keep furnishing the members of the commission with additional statistics as they are compiled. It appears now that counsel representing the Government are not prepared to go on with the material that has been furnished, and they suggest that there should be some further delay. On the other hand, counsel represent- I
ing Alberta and Saskatchewan says that he is here ready with witnesses. If seems to me the manifest duty of the commission is to hear these witnesses. . .
Then at page 4101 I quote:
Hon. Mir. Mabee: It does not make any difference whether some evidence is given to-day and some next week or whether the evidence that is given to-day is contradicted later on. I think there is no doubt at all that we should go on with the inquiry and get something done.
As a result of the decision given by the commission, Mr. Cowan, lep resen ting the two provinces, was allowed to put in certain evidence, and he immediately proceeded on the 16th of April to call three witnesses, namely:	W. R. Mclnnes, general freight traffic manager of the Canadian Pacific railway; J. D. Aiundel, general superintendent of the Ontario division of the Canadian Pacific railway, and George H. Shaw, general traffic manager of the Canadian Northern railway. Let me give briefly what counsel, representing the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, was able to establish out of the mouths of these tiaffic experts of the railway companies before the Board of Railway Commissioners. I shall not go into details, but I shall put in succinct form what was actually proven by the evidence of the railway officials tnemselves: In the first place it was proven that freight rates charged by railway companies west of Port Arthur were from twenty-five per cent to one hundred percent higher than the rates charged in Ontario and Quebec; in the second place it was proven from the records of the Canadian Pacific railway that the actual cost of hauling one thousand tons of freight one mile was less in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta, than in Ontario and Quebec; in the third place it was proven that the cost of maintenance of lines in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta was $400 less per mile than in Ontario and Quebec; in the fourth place it was proven that the actual transportation expenses were $434 less per mile of road in Saskatchewan and Alberta than in the eastern division of the Canadian Pacific railway; in the fifth place it was proven that taking the total of all operating expenses it costs $863 less per mile to operate railways in Saskatchewan and Alberta than in Ontario and Quebec; and in the sixth place it was proven that the density of traffic was twenty-nine per cent greater in Manitoba and sixteen per cent greater in Saskatchewan and Alberta than in' Ontario and Quebec.
In view of such facts being established, it is very difficult for a man who perhaps does not understand much about railroading to see what possible defence the railway companies could have to the fact that freight rates are so much higher in western

than in eastern Canada. I refer to section 77 of the Railway Act:
Whenever it is shown that any company charges one person, company, or class of persons, or the persons in any district, lower tolls for the same or similar goods, or lower tolls for the same or similar services, than it charges to other persons, companies, or classes of persons, or to the persons in another district, or makes any difference in treatment in respect of such companies or persons, the burden of proving that such lower toll or difference in treatment, does not amount to an undue preference or an unjust discrimination shall lie on the company.
On the 16th of April the Railway Commission took advantage of this provision and ordered that the onus of justifying these discriminatory freight rates was upon the railway company. In spite of that fact, three prominent lawyers of this country, acting on behalf of the Dominion Government have, according to the records of the Railway Commission, done practically nothing up to the present time to further this investigation. What is the reason ? I have seen rather ugly rumours in the newspapers as to the connection of some of these Dominion Government counsel with some other institutions in this country. I do not wish to refer to those matters to-day. Members of the Government have also seen the reports. If the people of Canada are to have any confidence in this Government and in our Railway Commission, something must be done to further the investigation which has now been pending before the commission for a year and a half with no result to the people of western Canada.
The meeting of April 16, 1912, was the most important meeting held on this question. A further meeting was held in Toronto on May 1, 1912, at which the Dominion Government counsel did the only thing which they have done in connection with this investigation. They filed certain exhibits which they got printed in the city of Winnipeg. On May 1, Mr. James Bicknell and Mr. H. W. Whitla were able to do this. These exhibits did not give any new information to the commission; they were merely supplementary to the exhibits already filed by counsel for the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta. Another meeting was held on May 21, 1912, and nothing was done. At that meeting Mr. Cowan, when asked as to whether or not he was ready to go on, said that he was ready to go on at any time. On June 18, another meeting of the commission was held at which this matter was mentioned. I wish it to be understood that I am not criticising the action of the Railway Commission, because the men who have charge of the investigation are the counsel for the Dominion Government. I believe the men on the Rail-Mr. MARTIN (Regina).
way Commission are the best men that we have in Canada. At a meeting of June 18, 1912, after the order had been made by the Railway Commission shifting the onus of proof on to the railway companies of justifying these discriminatory freight rates, what do you suppose that Mr. Jaimes Bicknell did? He asked the Railway Commission to hold meetings throughout the western provinces in order to see what the people might have to say about the freight rates. The Railway Commission said they would do that, in spite of the fact that they had all the evidence before them and that it had been amply established by evidence of railway officials that freight rates were 25 to 175 per cent higher than in eastern Canada. The Railway Commission went into western Canada for a period of three weeks and held meetings at the following places) Fort William, Winnipeg, Moosejaw, Regina, Saskatoon, Edmonton, Calgary, Vancouver and Victoria. I venture to say that the Railway Commission had filed with them between 150 and 200 complaints with respect to the these freight rates at that time. A further meeting was held on October 7, 1912, at which the railway companies commenced to put in evidence to justify their freight rates. Practically their whole defence was that freight rates at some points in the northern and western states were just as high as in western Canada. What kind of places do you suppose they cited? They took places like Thief River Falls in the state of Minnesota and Indian villages like Cheyenne in the state of Wyoming, places out of which there was practically no traffic at all, and they compared the freight rates at those points with the freight rates at great centres like the city of Winnipeg and distributing centres like Moose-jaw and Saskatoon and Regina. That is all the defence that they have put in up to the present time. The meeting of October 27, 1912 was finally adjourned and the commission met on January 7, 1913. I wish to refer to what took place at that meeting because it is the last meeting that has been , called in connection with that matter. At page 115 of volume 168 of the proceeding of the Railway Commission, Mr. Cowan made the following statement:
If the Chairman will adjourn until the morning, I will take up Mr. Melnnes then.
He is the freight traffic manager of the Canadian Pacific railway:
I do not want any misunderstanding, I am not in charge of this case. I am here acting for the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and I understand I must give way and I will very gladly to my learned friends the Dominion Government counsel. I suppose they are entitled to go on but the hoard very kindly let me step into it. So far as I am concerned I am prepared to take up at any time to-

morrow morning the cross examination of Mr. Mclnnes.
At the conclusion of that hearing, page 655 of the records, Mr. Whitla, one of the counsel for the Dominion Government, said:
The preparation of this case is proceeding with all rapidity

He is the gentleman who stated in the month of March, 1902, that he would be ready to go on in two or three weeks:
-and as I am advised, swiftly drawing to a conclusion. The latest advice, however, which I have received is in the shape of a telegram this morning from our experts and I am able to say that our case will be ready for presentation to the board in about six weeks time.
Nothing further has been heard of this case since the adjournment on January 7, 1913. The closing words of the chief commissioner at that meeting are somewhat instructive:
The Chief Commissioner: Well, Mr. Cowan, what is your position. Do you want to put in anything at all as to reasonableness of rates ?	.
Mr. Cowan: No, Mr. Chairman, the hoard's case was adjourned for my convenience to cross examine on A and B but engagements which were then hanging on me have now got behind and the western freight rates case has stepped up to the front. All my engagements will give way to the western rates case and to the convenience of the counsel in the ease. I am ready to go on at any time. *	*
Then, Mr. Cowan, on page 653 stated:
I will he ready when anybody else is able to go on.
That practically completes everything that I have respecting meetings held by the Railway Commission in connection with this matter.
I wish to emphasize one or two points once more before resuming my seat. What, according to the records, has the counsel employed by the Dominion Government been doing up to the present time? They have been doing absolutely nothing. If it had not been for the fact that some of the western provinces were represented on their own account, I am free to say that nothing at all wou/ld have been done. The Dominion Government counsel are employed by this Government and are supposed to be acting in the interest of the people of western Canada. Up to the present time they have not done so because, whenever the railway companies ask for an adjournment the Dominion Government counsel have been quite prepared to ask for an adjournment also. They are not ready to go on at the present time. If this freight rate investigation is delayed, if a decision is not arrived at within a short period of time, the responsibility for that delay rests
upontheDominion Government counsel and therefore upon the Government of the day I shall not go into figures to show all that that means tothe people of the West; but just let me give an example or two! Two or three years ago, the Regina freight rates case was pending before the Railway Commission. That case was taken before the commission in order to deal with discriminations that existed between the city °f Toronto and the city of Regina and other points in Saskatchewan and Alberta when compared with rates from Toronto to Winnipeg. The commission issued an order to the effect that on the 1st of April, 1910, the railway companies must furnish a new set of rates with respect to certain classes of commodities. That order was appealed by the railway companies to the Supreme Court of Canada. The Supreme Court upheld the decision. But I am told that up to the present time the railway companies have not complied with that order. They have furnished a new schedule of freight rates on certain commodities, it is true, but, according to business men in the city m.iW ,!ch -1 resic,e' they have not complied with the intention of the order of the commission. The point I make is that the question of freight rates means millions to Jh® province of Saskatchewan alone. Take that Regina freight rate3 case which affects only certain commodities. I am told that Mr. Lanigan said: If you can delay it for f T®ar ** wi!1 mean a million and a half to the Canadian Pacific railway alone The business men te.ll me that it means three millions in one year to the people of Saskatchewan _ alone. _ And the freight rates case that is pending now is much larger and far-reaching than the Regina case. If the decision of the Railway Board is delayed for one year, thus postponing the reduction of freight rates in western Canada it means millions to each of the three western provinces every year. Under such circumstances, I hope no one will blame me for bringing the subject to the attention of the House. The records of the Railway Commission go to prove that the Dominion Government, through its counsel, is simply temporizing with the investigation into the subject of western freight rates. I have shown that the investigation commenced a year and a half ago and I have proved by the records that nothing has been done up to this moment.
It has always seemed to me very peculiar that the manufacturers of eastern Canada did not take greater interest in freight rates on commodities going into the West. The manufacturers of eastern Canada wish to preserve western Canada as their market.
I do not blame them. But I can tell them that one of the greatest obstacles to their retaining the western markets is high

freight rates charged on commodities going into that country. How can any person in the province of Ontario blame a western man for buying an article from the United States when the distance over which that article has to be carried is only one-third, and the freight rates far lower? I do not wish to deal with the question of reciprocity, but to my mind, the great benefit of reciprocity would have been that the western farmers would have had a nearer market and lower freight rates on which they bought, and also a benefit through sending his grain to the American market for the same reason. However, I do not wish to be drawn into a discussion of that question.
As I said at the outset, I do not wish to be considered as criticising the action of the Eailway Commission. I am not doing that so far as I can help. But I will say that the Railway Commission up to the present time has occupied a position and enjoyed a reputation before the people of Canada that is sacred and inviolate. But if the people of western Canada are to be delayed for four or five years on the western freight rates question, I should be afraid the position of the commission will not be so sacred or inviolate at the expiration of that time as it is to-day.
I have already referred to section 77 of the Railway Act. All I have to say in conclusion is that I hope the Minister of Railways and Canals, or any other minister who replies to the statement I have made, will not use the arguments ordinarily put forward on behalf of this Government. The excuses are: First, you did it, or did not do it, as the case may be; second, we did not know it had happened; or, third, we have not had time to look into it. I hope we shall not hear any of these things from the Minister of Railways and Canals. I have great respect for the hon. minister and I do not suppose he would use any excuses of that kind in dealing with such a great question as that which I have brought before the House.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK COCHRANE (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
I suppose the hon. gentleman (Mr. Martin, Regina), thought that he was going to stop me from drawing the attention of the House to the fact that he sat in this House for three years before this Govern/nent came into power without bringing this subject before the Railway Commission. But he cannot get away from that fact. The late chairman of the Railway Commission, whose death we all deplore, and to whom I sent the complaint of the western farmers forwarded to me in January, 1912, replied that he had never had anything of the kind referred to him, nor had any request been made to him before to investigate it. I Mr. MARTIN (Regina).
have his letter on file, which I could produce to the House to substantiate that statement. I may say that the death of the late chairman undoubtedly had the effect of putting back this investigation. He had the matter in hand, and the appointing of the new chairman and the great quantity of work placed before the board, naturally had the effect of causing some delay. But I do not think that anyone will find fault with the present chairman. I believe that our predecessors in office were particularly happy in the chairman they appointed, for he proved himself a great servant of the people of Canada. And I have great pleasure in saying, that judging by what has been accomplished in the last few months, the present chairman will prove the equal of any of his predecessors, which is saying a great deal. I might remind the hon. member for Regina of the investigation which was referred to the Railway Board in 1904, and on which no ruling was made until 1910. I refer to the investigation into the subject of express rates. And I may say that when they did bring in their ruling there was no reduction of rates. Since the present chairman took up the case of western freight rates, he has issued an order that express companies, operating west of Sudbury shall reduce their rates by twenty per cent, and he has been in office for only a few months. I understand the railways put in a statement only about two months ago, and tljat the counsel for the Government has been getting experts from the United States, traffic experts, in order to go over that statement and establish his case. This is not a question that can be dealt with in a month; if it is dealt with in a year they will do well. This is a serious question and one that the present Government and the present board have given attention to. We are not humbugging or delaying over this matter, notwithstanding what the hon. member for Regina has said.

I am glad to hear from the Minister of Railways and Canals that at least the Government are taking this question seriously. We appreciate the hon. minister's statement that a large matter of this kind cannot be brought to a successful conclusion in a very short time. But the minister has not explained some of the statements, made by the hon. member for Regina in this connection. At a certain sitting of the Board of Railway Commissioners in the spring of 1912, over a year ago, the counsel representing the Government and the people before the commission stated that in two or three weeks they would be prepared to go on with the case. The minister has not told us why that counsel has been unable to go on with the case

for over a year since that time. The appeal of the hon. member for Regina to the minister was, as hon. gentlemen observed, an appeal in vain; but that was not unexpected, for we are getting used to the arguments used by members of the Government when they rise to defend their course in regard to any particular matter. The matter of an investigation into the freight rates of western Canada was definitely placed before the Board of Railway Commissioners nearly one year and a half ago. As the minister says, things can not he done all at once, but it does seem strange that the railway companies, who compile their statistics regularly, month by month, throughout the year, have been unable to lay before the Board of Railway Commissioners complete statistics with reference to the cost of transportation throughout the different provinces of Canada, especially in view of the fact that that information is undoubtedly on file in the head offices of the railway companies of this country.
I do not intend to add very much to what has been said by the hon. member for Regina, except to point out that, notwithstanding what the minister has said about the importance of this investigation-and it is because of its importance that we are so insistent that something should be done -it seems to be a strange thing that the counsel for this Government have seen fit to incur a delay extending over almost a year and a half in respect of an investigation the foundation of which information is in the possession of the head offices of the various railway companies of this country. What is the object of sending traffic experts to the United States? We are discussing the matter of freight rate discrimination in the Dominion of Canada; the question before the Board of Railway Commissioners is the discrimination between the East and the West-speaking of these sections of Canada in a popular sense. We are dealing with the discrimination between the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, if you like, and the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. We cannot discover any data bearing on this matter by sending traffic experts from the Department of Railways across to the United States; we have that information at home; we have it in the head offices of the various railway companies in this country. After these definite complaints had been placed before the Board of Railway Commissioners, what was the advantage of sending them on an excursion, if you will, throughout the western provinces of Canada? And now we are told that traffic experts are to be sent to the United States to obtain additional information. More than a year ago the counsel representing the provinces of Saskatchewan
and Alberta, Mr. Cowan, of Toronto, definitely proved before the Board of Railway Commissioners that there was an enormous discrimination in the rates charged in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta as against those charged in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. The various witnesses-themselves railroad officials-who were examined- by Mr. Cowan also demonstrated that in the prairie provinces the cost of railroad maintenance and operation was less than in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. There was a prima facie case absolutely proven by the statement of the traffic experts of the railways themselves. I contend that immediately upon that evidence being brought before the Board of Railway Commissioners, the Dominion Government's counsel should have said to the railways: Here is evidence which you have yourselves adduced, showing that your rates discriminate against the eastern provinces of Canada; upon you rests the onus and responsibility of demonstrating to the Board of Railway Commissioners why that discrimination exists. That, I say, was the responsibility resting there and then upon the counsel representing this Government, or, rather I should say appointed by this Government to represent the great consuming population of Canada. But the Dominion Government's counsel did not take advantage of the evidence adduced by the counsel for the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, but rather aided the railways in the delay which they undoubtedly desired in connection with this investigation. And why ? The executives of this Government are responsible for the appointment of that counsel; to them that counsel must furnish reasons for the delay. Notwithstanding what the Minister of Railways has said to-day, the public generally are persisting, and will persist, in asking the question: For what reasons are the Dominion counsel for the Board of Railway Commissioners delaying the investigation of this matter ? The minister says that the railways have not that information ready. I would remind hon. gentleman that there is apparently no delay in the companies obtaining the information necessary to decide the dividends they are going to pay to their stockholders year by year. As I understand the matter, the whole question of operating expenses and gross and net earnings has to be taken into consideration when those dividends are from time to time declared, so that the minister's argument that the railways did not get the information until two months ago, in my judgment, absolutely falls to the ground.
The hon. member for Regina has mentioned that the public are becoming suspicious that there is something wrong about this matter. We all appreciate the usefulness of the Board of Railway Com-

missioners to the people of Canada, and we all -recognize the ability of the personnel of that board. I have no criticism to offer of the present chief commissioner, because from the evidence submitted it appears that the board are not to blame, but that the counsel who represent this Government are the ones upon whom rests the responsibility for the delay in connection with this investigation. The Board of Railway Commissioners hold a high place in the esteem of the people, but the public are suspicious that there are reasons why this investigation is not being proceeded with other than those given by the Minister of Railways. I am not going to draw any inferences. The public press have stated the grievances and complaints of the people along this line. I am sure that these gentlemen, appointed as Dominion counsel, undertook that responsibility with the intention of carrying out their instructions. They are surely acting in sympathy with the wishes of those who appointed them, and if there is delay and protracted delay, without any justifications or excuse or reason being given for that delay, I say that the public are absolutely justified in concluding that the men who are responsible for that delay are not the counsel themselves but the men or the body whom they represent. The condition of affairs brought out in the evidence submitted to that commission through the question" of the counsel appointed by the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta must surely convince this House that the case before the commission is the most important that has been brought before that board since its inception. It is the most important case because that evidence, adduced from the mouths of the traffic experts of the various railway companies, absolutely proved to the people of this country that the people of western Canada are being illegitimately robbed, year after year, of millions of dollars by discrimination in freight rates. The people of western Canada are not radicals or anarchists or anything of that kind, but a condition of affairs such as this is surely enough to raise the ire of the most patient of people and I wish to tell the Government frankly that if they allow this state of affairs to continue, when they next appeal to the people of western Canada, they will be told in no uncertain voice what those people think about this pernicious delay for which the Government must certainly be held responsible. I tell the Minister of Railways frankly, notwithstanding the somewhat meagre applause he obtained from men behind him, that he will have to give this House and the country some better reason and some more extensive information as to a valid -reason for this delay before he wil1 ssfisfv us that there is not somewhere ' a nigger in the Mr. NE-ELY.
woodpile ' in connection with the procrastination in this investigation.

If the Government has no better defense to offer against the charge of bad faith in regard to a matter of stupendous importance to a very large portion of the people of Canada than has been offered by my hon. friend the ^mister of Railways, it will be in order for me to support in some degree the arguments that have already been placed before the House.
I want first of all to urge upon the House that this is not merely a western matter. All Canada is to-day aware that what affects adversely the producer of western Canada affects adversely every business interest throughout Canada. That every cent that is added to the value of the western farmer's product goes into circulation through the general channels of trade and finance throughout this whole Dominion. I do not think anybody will deny that because the return to the western farmer during the years 1911 and 1912 have not been up to expectations or to the realizations of the previous years, the interests of commerce, of industry, of finance and of transportation . throughout eastern Canada have been correspondingly adversely affected.
In this case the charge is that the transportation interest in western Canada takes more than its fair share out of the production and earnings of the people. If that charge is correct, then the interests of commerce and finance and industry of eastern Canada must suffer correspondingly. So that these interests are intimately concerned in the question that is before the Railway Commission to-day and that has now been brought to the attention of this House. I need not discuss at length the details of the question or prove what has been stated and has not been denied-although the minister responsible for the department has been on his feet and has had the opportunity to deny the statement if it was not correct-that is, the statement that there Is absolute and great discrimination in freight as between eastern and western Canada, contrary to the provisions of section 77 of the Railway Act.

Is there any greater
discrimination than there was in 1909, 1910 and 1911?

I do not think my hon.
friend is doing himself or his Government justice.
No, but you were not either.

Perhaps I was not, but I am not a member of the Government at the present time. I am not charged with the

responsibility of protecting the interests and rights of the people of Canada. My hon. friend is-he and his colleagues. It matters not to the people of Canada to-day whether I did right or wrong a year or a year and a half or two years or ten years ago. It really is not seriously important to the people of Canada whether I am doing right or wrong to-day. But it is important to the people of Canada whether my hon. friend and his colleagues are justly discharging the responsibility which has been laid upon them and protecting the interests of the peopl-e of Canada, or a large section of the people of Canada, according to the terms of the statutes of Canada.
The statement has been ' made and has not been denied that section 77 of the Railway Act is contravened by the conditions as they exist to-day in western Canada in regard to transportation. The responsibility on the Government is either to amend that Act, or to enforce it. If there is any reason in their minds why section 77 of that Act should not remain in the form in which it is, it is for them to stand up in their places in this House and take the responsibility of saying so. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that when a statute, plainly worded, is being notoriously contravened, it is not the place of the Government to attempt to shelter themselves behind the reputation of the Railway Commission. Aa my hon. friends on thia side have already said, it is not the Railway Commission that is in question to-day, it is not the facts that are in question to-day, it is the good faith of the Government that is at issue, in regard to actions of the counsel that they have seen fit to employ to push this investigation on behalf of the people of Canada. I do not know what the ideas of the Government are in regard to their duties, but these gentlemen are paid enough to give their whoie time and attention to this work. I submit that the question is important enough to call for their whole time and attention. Perhaps my hon. friends opposite would be interested to know that one of these counsel, Mr. Morrison, was a candidate in the recent elections in Alberta. It is true that he was not a very successful candidate. But the evidence is that he was as good a candidate on behalf of the Conservative party in Alberta as he is a solicitor or counsel on behalf of the people of Canada before the Railway Commission. I may mention that he was defeated by some 400 votes.
My hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely) and also my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin) has drawn attention to the fact that the railway companies have laid evidence before the Railway Commission in regard to freight rates prevailing in the western parts of the United States, instituting comparisons be-
283}
tween those rates and the rates prevailing in western Canada. And my hon. friend from Humboldt has said, that counsel for the Government before the Railway Commission also proposed to consider this question of freight rates in the western States as compared with those in western Canada. If that has any meaning at all, it means that the Government of the day, through their counsel, are lending their countenance to the proposition that it is right and proper- and that it is not discrimination under the Act-if railway rates in western Canada are higher than they are in eastern Canada so long as they are not higher than they are in the western States. If the railway companies are not losing their time entirely by presenting this evidence, it means that in this matter of western freight rates the Government of this country are proposing to take the same position as has been taken by our kings of finance, the bankers, who claim that the western farmer and the western man generally, should pay more for the same service than the people in other parts of Canada. I want to protest here and now against any such discrimination. I protest on behalf of the western part of Canada that the farmer, the rancher, the merchant, the miner, or whoever he may be, is entitled to the protection of the statutes whether he lives east or west of lake Superior.
It is the privilege of this Government to deny the suggestion if they desire to do so, but by allowing their counsel to dally with the question for a whole year and a half, the circumstantial evidence is that in the mat-of freight rates they have placed themselves on the side of discrimination against western interests. It is for them to clear themselves of the suspicion-no, not the suspicion, but to give a reason for that condition of facts-and I submit that they have not given such a reason. It is up to them to give a reason that will have weight and effect, and to show that they are prepared to see that the people west of lake Superior get that consideration and justice under the terms of the Railway Act which that Act was framed and passed by this Parliament to give them.
Let me point out to my hon. friends that the Railway Act was passed by their predecessors, and that the Railway Commission was established by their predecessors. This matter was before Parliament over a year ago, when it was discussed, so that they cannot plead that they had not heard of the matter, at any rate. We propose to insist that the importance of this case is such that it demands a settlement, and a settlement on the terms of the Railway Act, in accordance with the principles of that Act and in accordance

with the interests of the people of western Canada, and of Canada as a whole.

I do not want to intrude into western affairs, but happening to read a local newspaper published in my own town, the thought suggested itself to me that the people of the West will soon wake up to what hon. gentlemen opposite did when they were in power and to what the present Government have been doing since they came into power to alleviate their condition. Everyone who has paid any attention to the question of the transport of grain from the western provinces knows that year after year the people there had their grain kept in what elevators could be filled and in their granaries because the elevator accommodation at Fort William and Port Arthur was limited. Year after year-to my knowledge for ten or fifteen years-it was proposed that the Government of hon. gentlemen opposite should allow American vessels to go into Port Arthur and Fort William at the close of navigation and be practically floating elevators. But hon. gentlemen opposite were afraid to do so, because they were menaced by the friends of a few Canadian vessel owners who were politically friendly to them. The ex-Minister of the Interior knows that for years it was contended that in order to alleviate the condition of the farmer in the West, American vessels should be allowed to go in there, fill up with grain, lie there through the winter at floating elevators, and then come out in the early spring. The ex-Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) may have been favourable to that, but he was always over-borne by some person in the Cabinet. The same representation was made last fall to the present Government, and I want to say here that the grain situation was relieved last year in Manitoba and the Northwest territories to a greater extent than it had been for some years preceding. And why? It is because the present Government took the bull by the horns and they told the Canadian vessel owners, whether it pleased them or not, that American vessels were to be allowed to go into Fort William and fall up with grain. Does my hon. friend from Edmonton approve of that policy, which was adopted by this Government last fall?

I would say yes; and
now may I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

I have not the data
under my hand, but I am sure that there was always such a pressure in the West that there could not have been a year when every bushel of elevator accommodation was not taxed to the utmost at Fort William.

Then I submit to my hon. friend this information:	that there may
have been a very occasional year when that happened, but the general condition was that the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur were not taxed to their full capacity in any winter previous to 1912.

That seems a very extraordinary condition of affairs. Here were the farmers of the West, as described by these gentlemen opposite time and again, with their grain piled up in the fields rotting, and here were huge elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur ready to receive that grain.
The trouble was the diff-ficulty of getting the grain to Fort William and Port Arthur on account of the car shortage.
And it was just as bad last year.
No, it was not.

first and foremost. The railroads, which have built lines in western Canada, have been assisted to a great extent by the people of this country, and it is high time that the people should dictate to the railroads just what freight rates and other charges they should impose. No matter what party is in power, there must be greater control of railroads, especially when we are giving them assistance year in and year out. The railroads in western Canada are doing good business and are making money, but they are not expanding more quickly than they should. There are laTge sections of territory in western Canada without railway facilities where railroads have been promised and not provided. In those sections we have discontented people. This Government should set to work to alleviate that condition. It is a matter of importance not only to western Canada but to Canada as a whole. The prosperity and advancement of western Canada means also the prosperity and advancement of eastern Canada and of the whole Dominion.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
I rise simply to say a word or two in connection with what appears to be an implied statement of certain hon. gentlemen opposite throughout their arguments that there was some ground through which they might be able to fasten upon this Government some evidence of bad faith in the administration of the affairs of western Canada in so far as railway facilities are concerned. I absolutely deny that it is possible for any man, either in this House or outside of it, to establish the slightest tittle of evidence of bad faith on the part of the present Administration in carrying out a policy that means to the people of western Canada all the advantages that it is possible to bring to them in connection with the reduction of railway freight rates or the construction of railroads.
We have heard a good deal in regard to the matter of counsel who have had charge of this important case. We all recognize the vast importance of the question that has been submitted to the Railway Commission for their consideration. It is a very broad question, and representative counsel were selected to represent the Government and the people of this Dominion before the Railway Commission. We have also heard something of the counsel appointed by the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta. Would Mr. Cowan or Mr. anybody else have been here before the Railway Commission if the same policy as had been adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite had been carried on? Hon. gentlemen opposite say now that bad faith is shown; that delay is shown by the action of the counsel appointed in connection with this important case. Had it not Mr. BUCHANAN.
been for the change of government, we would not have had the necessity for these counsel; we would have had the same condition that existed for fifteen years when it was impossible for the farmers and merchants and people of western Canada to obtain the slightest relief at the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite when they governed this country. The hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) has told us today that, shortly after he was sworn in as Minister of Railways and acting upon the very first petition he received from the people of western Canada registering their complaints in respect to high freight rates, he took the only course that a minister in his place could take to provide a remedy. He transferred the request of those people to the Railway Commission. It was then headed by Mr. Justice Mabee, who drew attention to the fact that that was the first request which he had had during all the time he was chairman to undertake to deal with and to remedy the grievances of the farmers of western Canada. This is a very large question and it has taken considerable time before the Railway Commission. Unfortunately Mr. Mabee died and some time was lost before his successor was appointed. I am glad to know that his successor maintains the high standing of that commission before Parliament and the people of Canada. I am sure, as was evidenced by the fact the other day when he brought down his judgment in respect to the question of express rates and furnished a reduction to the people of western Canada of 20 per cent, that he will give the same effective consideration to the question of railway freight rates. He has much to do and much study to give in order to understand this great question.
My hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin) referred to the fact that the commission sat in the city of Regina discussing the question of railway freight rates; that they had before them representatives of the different railway companies, and the argument put before the commission on that occasion by the learned counsel representing the Grand Trunk Pacific railway was to the effect that it was impossible for his company to meet any reduction that might be imposed upon them by the Railway Commission owing to the fact that their line of railway had cost such an extraordinarily laTge amount for its construction. We have always claimed that this was caused by mismanagement, and therefore this is a principal reason for delay by the Railway Commission and by the counsel in order that they may give full consideration to the circumstances and conditions that make it impossible for the Grand Trunk Pacific railway to meet these rates, and in order that they may come to a decision as speedily as possible in the interests of the people of western Canada. I

have every confidence that this matter will be dealt with fairly and speedily by the Railway Commission. They are giving the matter full consideration. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals has told you that it is only two months since they got all the evidence the railways had to place before them, and they are having this evidence analysed and giving it the careful deliberation that it should have before giving a finding. For, you must recollect that while we in western Canada are most desirous of having a regulation of freight rates, we are equally, and if possible even more, interested in having extension of railways in many parts of the prairie provinces fox the convenience of farmers who are settling in those localities. Therefore, the greatest possible care has to be taken by the Railway i Commission before they reach a finding, to be certain that it will not hamper the construction of railways that are such an absolute necessity for the advancement and development of the West.
Now, I do not know that hon. gentlemen opposite touched on any other pomt. It is true that -when they were in power they did not supply, or undertake to supply, any relief to the people of western Canada regarding the question of freight rates. I remember in the years 1900, 1901 and 1902, the Government of the province of Manitoba saw that it would be necessary to find relief from the exorbitant rates that were being charged by the railways at that time. Finding that they could get no support from the Parliament of Canada, that Government undertook to make, and did make, a contract for the carrying- of grain over the distance of 300 miles from Winnipeg to Port Arthur, and in that connection undertook a heavy obligation. The result has been that millions upon millions have been saved every year to the people of Manitoba. In addition to the advantages secured by that contract to the province of Manitoba, there were large benefits also to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. These provinces had the opportunity^ to make similar contracts. They were giving guarantees to the railways to secure the construction of certain lines; but they did r-.ot provide In their contracts that they should have any control of railway freight rates in that country. They did not follow the example that we laid down in Manitoba which has done so much for the people of that province and for the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan. They followed, perhaps, rather the dictates and wishes of the railway people.

Was it not decided by the Railway Commission, and subsequently upheld by the Supreme Court, that the contract made by the Manitoba
Government was ultra vires of that province?

No, quite the opposite. My hon. friend is entirely wrong. The then Minister of Railways, Mr. Blair, when it was submitted to this House, acknowledged that we had full and complete power under our contract to provide relief for our own people; and that it was a good valid contract is evidenced by the fact that it is standing to-day and the people of western Canada are getting the full benefit of it.

I do not wish to inturrupt the hon. minister, but I would like to ask a further question. Apparently, I am astray in my facts. Since the Railway Commission was established, is it not true that similar contracts are restricted?

I do not think it is beyond the powers of any province to make a contract with a railway company that will afford relief to the people it represents, I believe the provinces have absolute power in that matter; we found it so far as the province of Manitoba is concerned. Let me add that, so far as I know, the present Dominion Government are giving through their Minister of Railways and Canals, full and careful consideration to this wide and very important question, and I am satisfied that when the matter has been thoroughly gone into and investigated by the Railway Commission neither this Parliament nor the people of western Canada will have any fault to find with the action of the Government or of the commission. I trust that the long and careful investigation of the matter will result in great advantage to the people of western Canada.

I do not wish to delay the House for more than a few minutes. I would like to say a word before my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) leaves the Chamber. I was extremely interested in hearing the advice he gave that the late Government should have said to some people south of the line: Come on with your American boats. I have understood that my hon. friend was one of a party of men elected to this House on the ery, 'No truck or trade with the Yankees,' -and on the declaration that it would be ruinous to Canada if the lines of our business ran north and south instead of east and west. I offer him congratulations on the fact that light is breaking in a somewhat unexpected quarter.
I have -been interested in the statement made by the ministers who have spoken on this occasion, and I am anxious to take as much consolation as I can for myself and for my fellow farmers, out of the assurance of the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Railways that this mat-

ter is commanding the serious attention of the Government and that it will be gone on with with all possible expedition and energy. I think that is the assurance I had from these hon. ministers, and am very glad to have it; and I want to get as much consolation as possible from it. I wish they had given us that assurance without dealing with this question as a party question. I fail to see evidence on the part of the Government, so far as their spokesmen are concerned, of a due appreciation of the economic conditions of the West. On one point the Minister of Public Works proved himself an extremely bold controversion-alist. He had said, as I understood: It is the first time that a matter of this kind has been inquired into at all. He seemed to wish to take credit to the Government for this fact. I venture to repeat that my hon. friend is extremely bold on this point as a controversalist on this, one of the few occasions when he has favoured the House with his political wisdom. The late Government appointed ttie Railway Commission. We will give them credit for that at any rate. I have said, I do not want to deal with this as a party question, but when it is put before us by two responsible ministers apparently as a party question, one cannot help dealing wuh what they advance. The late Government appointed the Railway Commission. The hon. Minister of Public Works was not responsible for that; he was not a member of that Government; he would not have been eligible. This commission began an investigation into a condition which became accentuated after the present Government came into power; and the Minister of Public Works says: What a good Government we have that is in office when this inquiry is made. My information is that the inquiry was not ordered by the Government, but by the commission appointed by the late Government. That is the kind of point the hon. gentleman puts forward. I hope he will try to see the spirit of it and how it will be judged by the people of the West.

The hon. gentleman does not seem to understand that the investigation now being made by the Railway Commission is being made at the request of the Government.
'Mr. OLIVER: The Government appoint these lawyers, who are doing nothing.

If that be so, I am glad to hear it. I understood that the inquiry originated from the fact that the condition of affairs was pointed out to Parliament and to the Government-whether the late one or the present one-in a speech made by my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) in the spring of 1911. There is no Mr. CLARK (Red-Deer).
party question involved in this-and that is what I want to bring home to my hon. friends and to the Government-this is an economic question requiring more serious consideration than it seems to have obtained from hon. gentlemen opposite, 'if one is to judge from the remarks of the minister and others who have spoken on the other side.
As I have said, I do not want to occupy the time of the House for more than a few moments, but I would like to impress emphatically upon the Governments-and this was dwelt upon by my hon. friend from Regina in his opening remarks- that the condition of affairs in western -Canada at the present moment is a very serious one. That is the point which concerns the inhabitants of that part of this country, and, as has been pointed out by several speakers, that is the point which in the end concerns the whole of Canada, because if the western producers suffer, the eastern manufacturers will not be long in suffering also. This is not a question as between the two parties on the opposite sides of the House, and it is not a question as between eastern and western Canada; it is a question which affects the prosperity and the progress of our whole country, and if we could but rid ourselves of party spirit for a moment we would all try to approach it from that point of view and from that point of view alone. That this is a serious question is a statement which scarcely requires any proof by those who know the condition of affairs in the West to-day. I have been very much taken to task because in previous debates this session I have mentioned the serious conditions that prevail in western Canada, and I think that with many sections of the population one incurs very considerable risk in mentioning it, because one cannot forget that a very large number of the people of western Canada are there not to farm, but to speculate in real estate. The economic question, and the really serious question for the people of Canada to-day is the necessity for promoting the production of wealth within the country, and that is what I would like to impress upon every thoughtful [DOT] man in this House. Personally I believe that it can be proved that, with all our railway propagation in the last few years, we have had a very poor corresponding increase in the actual production of wealth within the country, and that is what is the matter with Canada at the present moment. I do not care what steps the Government take to remedy that condition, they are wise steps-whether along the line of traffic or along the line of transportation I will support them. I will support them in my own interests, in the interests of the great mass of producers in the West, and in the interests of the whole country.

I do not want to go back to the question ot reciprocity and to the arguments by which our opponents opposed it, but a kindred thought to the limited nature of our production at the present moment occurs in connection with this argument and with the great question of transportation. We all know the peculiar formation of our country. We have thousands of miles of rocks and trees; they are there, nature has put them there, and when nature places any obstacle in our way we want to take rational methods of overcoming it. Our friends say:	You have got to transport
your material from the East to the West- that is when we do not get a glimmer of light such as came from my non. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) just now- if you are raising steers, you must bring them across this great stretch of country and over Canadian railways. The sight of the rock will he good for the steers' constitution, I suppose; in any case, it is certainly good for hardening the beef and making it bring inferior prices in the British market. But what is the economic result of insisting so strongly upon that line of policy? It is that you cease to produce steers altogether; you are only producing a little more beef in this country than it is necessary for your own consumption at the present moment. I want to bring home to the minister the fact that this is not a question which necessitates the throwing of stones from one side of the House xo the other, and the statement that hon. gentlemen opposite have only been two years in office. I have extended to my hon. friends the utmost sympathy on that point, silent and expressed - very often expressed, I am afraid; it was necessary for me to do so from time to time. But it is not a question of how long we have been in office, or how long the other party were in office; as the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) said, this Government has suffered for its faults-they have gone out of power, and what we have got to see and what the present Government have got to see is that the people of Canada do not suffer with them. I do not want the present Government to do anything beyond their capacity, but they have got to live up to their capacity, and a mere exchange of party thrusts an3 darts will be very poor satisfaction to the men who, according to my own knowledge, are having a hard fight to make ends meet upon the prairie. It is true they have got their land, but they cannot eat land. We have an expression out there which refers to a man as being ' land poor '; it is perfectly possible for a man to be land poor. These men are having a hard fight; I know it by experience, and it will be a poor consolation to them that the present Government says to the party opposite:	You did as
little for them as we have done. The question before the House is a double one. It is asserted, in the first place, that there is a discrimination in freight rates as between eastern and western Canada. It appears to me	that it should not
take so very	long	for a	body
properly constituted to find out the facts of the matter. The hon. member for Regina was very courageous in his remarks upon this point, and he made a statement which was not given the slightest notice by the two ministers which have spoken; at least I listened very carefully to what they said, and I could not catch the slightest reference to that statement. He said that there is a tremendous discrimination-and I appeal very strongly to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, because he represents western Canada
That is what the Railway Commission are doing-investigating that very matter.
I am glad to have that assurance.
They are not investigating it.
You have said yourself that they were.

The fact that the Railway Commission are investigating it does not seem to me to excuse the minister from absolutely avoiding all reference to the q estion. If my hon. friends had even said that it was a serious thing that that discrimination should exist, it would have been some satisfaction to me, but they absolutely neglected to refer to the fact that it is being inquired into, and that will not do for the people of western Canada. They would like to be aware of the fact that the ministers are concerned to know whether or not there is a discrimination between the East and the West; thev would like to have tne assurance, in more than words, if possible. that there is not some truth in the suspicion of my hon. friend the member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) that the present Administration has more sympathy with the shareholder and the directors of the rai^ roads than tney have with the hard-working producers of wealth on the plains of western Canada. This question, from this point of view, is one which should surely appeal very strongly to every patriotic Canadian. It is constantly stated that eighty per cent of the shareholders of one great Canadian railway corporation live outside of Canada altogether, and it will be a lamentable day for Canada if we come to have a government in power who are more concerned about the size of the dividends paid to ihe eighty per cent of shareholders living entirely outside of Canada than they are as to the welfare of the producers upon their own plains.

Let me now refer briefly to the second question under debate-and here I would ask my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works to refer to the perfectly courteous interruption he made to my remarks a few moments ago. The inquiry is why the investigation which he says is going on at this moment was delayed. I do not think my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works touched upon that question; I never heard him utter a single word about the delay of the investigation, or whether it had taken place. It is either a fact that that delay took place, or it is not a fact; if the delay took place, the people have a right to be told why it took place. They will not be perfectly satisfied with the statement of the minister that the investigation is now going on at full speed. The Minister of Railways made a statement in this matter which consisted really of two sentences. He said in the first place that he was not going to be debarred by anything said by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin) from making the usual answer of the Government. If he had not, he would have been debarred from making any answer at all, because it is the only answer we have ever heard from this Government.
What about the comparison of the two investigations?

My hon. friend still wants to carry on the comparison. He was not here in opposition, but he is so little satisfied, apparently, with his efforts along the lines of constructive statesmanship that he puts himself in opposition in imagination and, instead of defending his own Administration, he spends his time in criticising the former Government. I ask him if he thinks that is worthy of his position as a minister? It is not worthy. The question is not the difference between the last Government and this, it is a-question whether there is any difference between the freight rates charged in the East and in the West. That is the point on which my hon. friend should concentrate his attention. What is he troubling about? Having got into office so recently is he afraid of losing it? I do not think the danger is altogether beyond the possibility of imagination, I think it is a considerable danger but dwelling on it all the time is not the way to avert it, it will increase it. The only way in which you will prevent yourself from being removed from office will be by putting up a policy that will be of some benefit to the people of Canada. That is the only point of difference, difference between the freight rates in the East and in the West and not difference between the last Administration and this.
