My hon. friend says they are looking into the matter. The Minister of Public Works made a similar statement, he was Mr. CLARK (Red Deer).
considering the matter. The Government are looking into so many matters that the people are beginning to doubt their powers of vision. That is what is the matter with hon. gentlemen of the Government so far as the political situation is concerned. One would naturally wish that the Government would see something when they look and do something as a result of what they see. A Government that looks and considers and does nothing may be tolerated until the next general election, but it will not be tolerated any longer. I have been giving the Government more or less advice this session with very bad results, they do not pay any attention to me, but I do hope that on this matter they try to do something to make a substantial reduction in these rates as against the people of western Canada and in that way help the producers who are building up the whole country.

Any person reading or listening to this debate will give the prize to my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) for making the most partisan speech in connection with it. I am sure the House and the country have heard quite enough from my hon. friend in the shape of lectures to this Government. My hon. friend never approached a debate in this House since this Government came into power without referring to the reciprocity question. He could not say a few words as he promised on this question without taking a thrust at the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett), who kept close to the mark, discussing this question of reduction of freight rates in the West. My hon. friend from Red Deer could not discuss this question without making comparisons between this Government and the late Government, in such a way that almost every sentence uttered by him was of the partisan type that he is constantly condemning in this House but in respect of which he is the greatest sinner who has been in this House for the last fifteen years.

Would my hon. friend quote
me?

Yes, I can quote my hon. friend. In this very speech, my hon. friend did not give one statement, he scarcely debated the question at all, he did not make any statements of complaint except the universal political complaint against this Government.
I quoted the hon. member for Regina. Why does not my hon. friend refer to him also?

I do not wish to say very much to my hon. friend for Red Deer. He is very kindly and courteous in debate ; but I am sure when he reads this speech he will cease lecturing the Government and pre-

tending to this House and the people of Canada that he is less of a partisan than those who sit around him. For my part, coming from the east of Canada, I have not heard anyone say very much in complaint about the West. If there is any division or cause of division or suggestion about division between the East and the West it comes from the people of the West, such as my hon. friend. If my hon. friend wishes to help the Government in bringing about reduced freight rates for the farmers and people of the West, why does he not compliment the Government for what they have already done since coming into office? My hon. friend had nothing to say about the twenty per cent reduction on express rates brought about by the influence of this Government in connection with the Railway Commission since they came into office; not a word of praise, not a word of compliment to the Government for what they are doing; and yet my hon. friend, a supporter of the late Government, a western farmer himself, athough freight rates in the West were not as he would like them, sat in his place in this House and the Chairman of the Railway Commission was able to make the statement that the first time this important question was brought to his attention to deal with was by the present Minister of Railways and Canals. My hon. friend surely was forgetting his duty, Why did not my hon. friend become as active when he was a supporter of the Government as he is now active as a member of the Opposition? Why did not my hon. friend turn up ' Hansard ' and quote where he himself in this House brought this matter to the attention of the Railway Board when he was a supporter of the late Government? My hon. friend, of course, could not do that because he was a hide-bound supporter of that Government in everything. I have under my hand some statements of his. I shall not read them now but I may at some future time.	,
Let us have them, they are good stuff.
Do not refer to them ii you cannot give them.

My hon. Mends referred to many things, and I do not want to get into any controversy. Any hon. gentleman looking at the record of this Government, after eighteen months in office, and what they have accomplished for the people of the West must have some praise to give to them.
Give a. few instances.
The twenty per cent reduction in express rates.

That investigation was
started before the present Government came into office.
It did not start until the present Chairman of the Board was appointed.
Even now the rates are not as low as in the East. [DOT]

They are not satisfied and will not give a word of praise to the Government. They have no word of commendation for that twenty per cent reduction which is a very large reduction in express rates, and I am sure it must be in the interests of the people of Canada, and particularly of the people of the West, because express parcels are being more numerously carried now, and there are more people taking advantage of express service than in years gone by. I rise simply to compliment the Government. When a member of this Government makes a plain, unvarnished statement that they are pressing the Railway Commission, and that the Railway Commission are actively engaged in getting information so that they will be able to bring about some reduction in freight rates, as they have done in express rates, for the West, it does not come with very good grace from hon. gentlemen opposite, those representing western constituencies in particular, to indulge in a partisan discussion such as we have heard to-day without giving credit to the Government for anything they have done for the benefit of the people of Canada.

As my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) an eastern man, has thought fit to butt into this debate, I may be pardoned if I say a few words. I hope my hon. friend will not consider me discourteous if I fad to follow him in his lecture to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. I want the House to get back to the real question under discussion. As I understand it, the claim has been put forth by many people in western Canada that the freight rates are unduly larger in the West than in the East. This matter was laid, not before the Government, but before the proper tribunal. One would imagine, listening to my hon. friend from Peel and to the hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) who, I think, was the greater sinner of the two, that the Government had something to io with this. The Railway Commission was created in 1903 by this Parliament. I do not caTe whether a Liberal Government cr a Conservative Government is entitled to the credit; the commission was created by the Parliament of Canada, and to it was given the exclusive right of dealing with freight rates. This Parliament has noth-

Did they reduce the
rates at all?

Yes, they did to some
extent, though I am bound to say that, in my judgment, they did not go so far as they should have gone. My hon. friend must remember that there has been only one or two changes on the commission. There has been one change caused by death, and one addition, and I believe we have just as good a commission to-day as we ever had. If the commission, in their judgment, found that they were justified in reducing express rates by twenty per cent, that only justifies the action of the late Government in appointing the Railway Commission, and justifies the present Government in maintaining it. So let us get away from all questions as to whether the late Government or the present Government are entitled to any credit, so far as the Railway Commission in the performance of its duty is concerned.
The charge has been made that there is a discrimination in rates. I have not gone into the facts, but I think the statement of the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin) is correct, because it has not been denied, and if it had not been true it would have been denied by the Minister of Railways. The statement is that the Railway Commission, the only tribunal capable of discussing this matter, has found, as a matter of fact, that the freight rates are discriminative. That is what I want my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals and the Minister of Public Works to consider for a few moments. The next Mr. CARVELL.
question is, should they be discriminative? I think that is the logical question to be answered.
If the commission has found that, as a matter of fact, as my hon. friend says, why does it not remedy the defect? That is in their power. Why should he blame this Government?

The next question
which should be discussed is, have the railway companies a right to make discriminative rates?

The commission is
there to cure that discrimination, if it exists.

The question of what
the freight rates should be on any road in Canada is the question to be considered. The railway companies should be allowed to charge rates on traffic which, after paying all running expenses, will yield a reasonable profit on the investment.

What about
fixed charges?

I include fixed charges. As a matter of fact, according to the statement of my hon. friend from Regina, the Railway Commission have found that the railways in the provinces of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan cost less per mile to build than the railways in the eastern provinces. The Railway Commission have also found as a matter of fact that it costs less per mile to operate them, than it does to operate the railways in eastern Canada. That is the statement made by my hon. friend from Regina, and it has not been contradicted; therefore, I assume these facts to be correct. Now the question arises, under that condition of facts as found by the Railway Commission, should the commission order the railway companies to reduce their rates? The railway companies say no. Then the Railway Commission says to them, if those rates should not be reduced, the burden is on you to convince us to that effect; you produce to us the evidence that will justify us in retaining those charges as they are; prima facie they ought to be reduced, because your railways cost less to build and to operate, and therefore the rates ought to go down. In other words you are taking from the people a rate that is more than necessary to pay the running expenses and fixed charges and to provide for a reasonable remuneration upon your investment. As I understand it, the whole charge is that the counsel representing this Govern

ment are the cause of the delay. It is not a question of whether this Government was justified in appointing counsel or of whether they are entitled to credit for anything that has been done by the Railway Commission. My hon. friend from

Regina has stated a case showing that, on account of the action of counsel representing the Government, the matter has been delayed for over a year. Now they say vve want to go to the United States to find out the conditions there. .

I did not say that
they were going to the United States for evidence. I said they were getting traffic men from the United States.
That is the same thing. My hon. friend is quibbling.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
According to Peel and
Brand, the use of the word ' quibbling ' is not permissible in Parliament.

If the word ' quibbling ' is unparliamentary, I will withdraw it, and say it is the difference between tweedledee and tweedledum. I say to my hon. friend the Minister of Railways that they have no right to go to the United States for evidence in respect to freight rates in Canada. My hon. friend knows that in the United States the railroads are built by men who put their own money into them. In some cases they have received slight assistance from municipalities, and possibly from states, but as a rule the railways of the United States are built by private enterprise and private capital, and those people are entitled to charge rates sufficient to yield a reasonable remuneration on their investment, after paying the cost of operation and maintenance. That is not the case in Canada. There is not a railway in Canada that has fifty per cent of private money invested in it. The Canadian Pacific railway has not twenty-five per cent of private money in it; in fact, I doubt whether it has ten per cent. It is true that during recent years the Canadian Pacific railway have been selling stock, mostly common stock, to their stockholders, and a certain _ amount of private money has been put into the corporation, but as against that, everybody knows they have received millions of dollars worth of land, and there is not a mile of their road that has not been subsidized by this Parliament to the extent of $6,000 or $7,000 per mile:

I may
tell my hon. friend that a line built last year from near Peterborough to Port Mc-Nichol, did not receive a cent.
How long is that road?
About 100 miles.

It will be here for a subsidy and it will get it; do not make any mistake about that. If my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) did not state that of his own knowledge, I would feel like denying it. Well, I think there is a good road in northern Ontario that did not receive a subsidy from this Government, but that is not the fault of the Government; the Government tried to give it a subsidy.
The Canadian Pacific railway from Toronto to Sudbury did not receive any grant from this Government, and it was a very expensive road to build.
My hon. friends opposite do not want to be too pernickity about this business; my statement is practically correct.
Correct enough for you.

If you go through Canada from one end to the other, you will not find more than two or three lines of railway not subsidized by this Government. My statement is practically correct that all the railways in Canada have been built out of public money. I do not think there is a railway in Canada to-day that has twenty-five per cent of its capital in actual money belonging to the private individuals who are shareholders of the road; these railways got land grants from this Government, subsidies from this Government, subsidies from the provincial governments, guarantee of bonds from this Government and the provincial governments, bonuses from the municipalities, and so on. They are all financed by the public and they are not in the same category at all with the railways in the United States. What would be true of the freight rates that might be charged in the United States would not be a criterion for proper freight rates in Canada. The Minister of Railways is putting up a very poor case when he justifies this delay by saying they are waiting to get evidence from the United States. The charge now is that counsel for the Government are not prosecuting this matter as vigorously as they should. There are three or four reasons which may account for that; one is that they are under the influence of the railways and I am not saying that is true. The other is, that they want delay for some reason, and I might almost go as far as to say that if the Government did not appoint men big enough for a big job, they will get delays as they get them in this case; another reason is that one of these gentlemen is running elections in Alberta. These are the complaints the Government have now to answeT, and not what they have done since they have been in power in reducing freight rates. The Minister of Public Works was going to reduce freight rates in the constituency of Macdonald some time last October; it was reported in the newspapers.
That was reported in the irresponsible press.

I notice the Minister of Public Works is willing enough to _ deny anything he can deny, and I am waiting to hear from him with respect to this. I su*' pose he thought he would make some votes in Macdonald, and no doubt he used the argument.

Where would the hon. gentleman suggest that the Railway Commission would get evidence of a disinterested character against the railways of this country if not from the United States? The evidence as to the cost of running railways in this country must come from the railways themselves, and they are all interested in the matter. I have considered many a time as to where such disinterested evidence would come from and I should like a suggestion from my hon. friend as to that. The shipper does not know, the consignee does not know what it costs to carry his freight, and if you confine yourself to getting evidence in Canada, you must obtain it from the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Northern or the Canadia,n Pacific railway, all of which are interested. Where wouM the hon. gentleman suggest that this disinterested evidence should come from if not from the neighbouring republic?
That is a fair question.

It has bothered me
for a good many years.

I frankly say I am not in a position to answer the question, but in my judgment, you do not have to go out of Canada. I believe the Railway Commission, if supported by counsel big enough for the job, could get all the evidence in Canada.
Prom what source?
From the railways themselves.
But they are all interested.

If the Railway Commission had counsel big enough and able enough, they would bring the Canadian Pacific railway into court with their books, and they would have practical railway men to assist them, and they would be able to find out from the books of the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk or the Canadian Northern, exactly what it costs to transport a ton of freight a mile, and what it costs to maintain the road, and what it costs to construct the road, and they will be able to form an intelligent opinion on that without going out of Canada.

The hon. gentleman
appreciates the difference between _ getting friendly evidence and evidence which you have to get out of an opposing withess by Mr. ROGERS.
cross-examination, and so on. There is a great difference between the two kinds of evidence.

The principle cited by
my hon. friend is true, that you should never rely upon an opponent's witnesses if you can help it. But there are different kinds of evidence and the evidence that is required in this case is not the opinion of witnesses but the facts which are in the possession of every railway company in Canada, who know exactly what it costs per ton to transport freight, to maintain the road, and to construct the road. There are dozens of counsel in Canada, who know enough about railway matters-I think my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) is one-to know exactly what books and documents you would want from the railway company to prove this. The Chairman of the Railway Commission has that knowledge, and he can put his finger on exactly the proper document he requires from any railway company in Canada, and he can make it bring that document into court to get at the facts. Mr. Cowan representing Alberta and Saskatchewan found enough to satisfy the Railway Commission that they should decide there was discrimination. Mr. Cowan proved out of the mouth of the witnesses of the railway companies that it cost less to construct a railway on the prairies than it did in the East, and that it cost less to operate a railway on the prairies than it did in the East. What more do you want? But through the dilatory tactics of counsel representing the .Dominion Government, there has been delay month after month during all this time. That is what we are finding fault with to-day. While I do not want to impute dishonourable motives to counsel representing the Government, I think something ought be done to hurry them up. It is all their fault. It is not for the Government to show that the rates are too high; it is for the railway companies to produce evidence to show that their rates should not be reduced. I am afraid hon. gentlemen opposite are approaching this matter from a political standpoint, rather than from a business standpoint. I think the hon. member from Regina deserves the thanks of every man in Canada for bringing this matter to the attention of the House. I hope that the Minister of Railways will spur them on, and, if they have' not sufficient ability or willingness to move fast enough, that he will get other men who will. There are plenty of lawyers in Canada who will take retainers from him and who will see the work done properly. If the railway companies are not able to furnish sufficient evidence to justify the present rates, let the counsel press the matter and get a decision from the Railway Commission. I have sufficient faith in the Railway Commission to believe that they

will give a verdict according to the evidence. The evidence will be that the rates should be reduced. If the Railway Commission do come to such a decision, I do not think my friends should find any fault, and I also do not think that their friends will be aggrieved, because they ought to be subject to the laws of the country just as the farmers of the Northwest are. I hope my hon. friend the Minister of Railways will see that this evil is abolished; that these people will bring the matter to a head and that the question will be decided upon its merits.

It is now fifteen years or over since I went to western Canada. At that time there was just one line of rail communication that was offering anything like transportation facilities to the people of this country; that was the Canadian Pacific railway. Since then we have had two railways projected. They are not yet completed to the coast. The question of freight rates has naturally engaged the attention of the people a great deal during that time. There has been agitation after agitation, as the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has: said, to reduce freight rates upon the Canadian Pacific railway, before competition was offered. The people of western Canada naturally expected that, when new roads were projected, some solution of the problem of the charges made for the carriage of traffic on railways would be offered. It must be remembered that the bonds of the Canadian Northern railway were guaranteed by this Dominion. The bonds of its branch line system are largely guaranteed by the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. The bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific main line have been guaranteed by this Dominion, and the mountain section was practically built by the Dominion. The branch lines of the Grand Trunk Pacific have been laid by the expenditure of money raised on guarantees of securities guaranteed by the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. One would naturally expect that one would find some solution offered by gentlemen, who for fifteen years had control of this country, of the vexed problem of excessive freight rates which the western farmers pay. What do we find to-day? The fixed charges of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company do not amount to $800 per mile or will not when they retire the securities that are now about maturing with the proceeds of the recent stock issue. The fixed charges of the Canadian Northern Railway Company amount to something like $1,000 per mile. The fixed charges of that railway which is the particular pet of the former Administration will amount to over $2,000 per mile for that portion extending from Edmonton to Winnipeg.

That will do twice the
business.

I am coming to that.
That being so, I ask the hon. gentleman from Carleton (Mr. Carvell):	What was
the first thing one had to think about in regard to freight rates ? Anyone who has studied railroads at all knows that the first factor in fixing freight rates is the fixed charges.	[DOT]

Do you ask me that as a
question?	,
Yes, if you desire so to construe it.

In my judgment, the
Grand Trunk Pacific railway is a much tetter proposition and can do business on a lower rate at $2,000 fixed charges per mile than the one per cent road on fixed charges of $1,000 per mile can do, for the reason that they can haul twice the traffic with the same engine.

The lack of knowledge of the hon. member for Carleton on the subject of railroads is greater than I thought it was.
The fixed charge is the first factor in fixing a freight rate. It therefore follows that, in order to find out what is a reasonable freight rate in western Canada, you must investigate the fixed charges of the three railroads that are carrying the traffic. That is obvious. The Canadian Pacific railway has been maintaining a freight rate in western Canada during all these years based upon one principle, which is the governing principle laid down by American roads and which was adopted in this country. Whenever the Canadian Pacific railway had a line to put into operation, it based its freight rates upon figures shown by the United States. Those figures, as we know, were based upon the traffic bearing all that it could carry. In other words the freight traffic should always pay all it could bear. We know that from the day of the first railway. In Canada we have the same nrincinle applied. In other words, the freight rate was just as large as it was possible to get out of the traffic that was carried by the railway.

The railways give the
farmers just enough to live upon and take the rest.

No, they charge just as much as the traffic will bear. My hon. friend from Carleton Shows a lamentable Jack of knowledge in regard to the matter of railways. He should have known that every transcontinental railway that crossed the United States or attempted to cross it went intp the hands of a receiver, except

the Great Northern; and that every one of the roads, including the Northern Pacific, the Union Pacific and the Southern Pacific, were subsidized with enormous land grants and cash, aggregating more than the subsidies-paid by the former Conservative Government to the Canadian Pacific railway. I should like to remind my hon. friend that the Liberal Government of the day offered the Caaadian Pacific railway fifty million acres of land to build the road and could not find a contractor who would undertake it, whereas the Conservative Government offered them twenty-five million acres and they took it. If he would like to see ihe advertisements which appeared in the newspapers of that day, I should be glad to show them to him in the library. We all know, of course, in the light of present day facts that too much was given to the Canadian Pacific railway. It is idle for a man at the present time, in the light of his present knowledge, to condemn the action that was then taken in view of the fact that men possessing the finest intellects of the day, for instance Edward Blake, said that the road would not earn sufficient to pay for grease for the. wheels.

My hon. friend has misunderstood me. I was offering no criticisms on any government for giving a land grant to the Canadian Pacific railway. I do not do so now. I am sorry that they have got it, and therefore they should not be allowed to charge enormous freight rates on account of it.

I quite appreciate what my hon. friend has -said. I was only pointing out the facts because he spoke of them having land worth $300,000,000. In fact, they had eighteen million acres of land left, reselling seven million acres to the Government, and I have never heard even my hon. friend from Edmonton place a value of three or four hundred million dollars on this land grant. Even in the light of our present day knowledge, the figures used by my friend from Carleton require a little pruning.
The next road was the Canadian Northern railway. That road is to-day laid with sixty pound steel from Winnipeg to Edmonton, with mud ballast and light ties. They fixed their traffic tolls at the same figures relatively as those which had been fixed by the Canadian Pacific railway. As they were carrying traffic. through the same territory, they naturally could not charge a larger freight rate.
Then came the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. They followed exactly what these other roads did and fixed the same tolls that were fixed and enjoyed by the other- two roads, as my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin) knows. In regard to the carriage of passenger traffic, we all know that that road, Mr. BENNETT (Calgary.
not being completely taken over from the contractors, has a very excellent service over a -limited mileage. As to whether or not it is paying, no man except the officials of the company knows, but the rates charged are substantially the same as those charged by the other roads.
There you have the freight rates situation in western Canada. You have to-day, the Canadian Pacific railway, a railway in the highest possible state of efficiency, very economically administered, as the figures show, compared with the railways in the United States; you have the Canar dian Northern railway, carefully and efficiently administered, but physically requiring the same kind of reconstruction that the Canadian Pacific railway had to undergo between the time when I first went' West fifteen years ago and the presenttime. Seven or eight years ago the Canadian Pacific railway was reconstructed, as the hon. member for Edmonton knows. The 56-pound rail, the 1,500 ties to the mile and the mud ballast gave way to the 80-pound rail, the 3,000 ties to the mile and the gravel ballast. The Grand Trunk Pacific, as the hon. member for Carleton has said, was built in the first instance, at a very very high standard of efficiency. In other words it was built with 80-pound steel, with 3,000 ties to the mile, and ballasted with stone and gravel. What follows? The first criticism the people of western Canada are offering is that the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Pacific railway traverse substantially for many miles between Edmonton and Winnipeg the same territory. They are not far enough apart. And it is not very hard to see by careful observation

observation that, I know, will be borne out by the hon. member for Regina if he will think about it for a moment- Grand Trunk Pacific trains going out with engine, roadbed and grades sufficient to enable 70 loads to be hauled, but actually hauling, perhaps, 20 loads, for the reason that they have not the traffic to carry. But the fixed charges upon that system must be paid. The agitation to reduce freight rates continues. When this Government came into power the Minister of Railways at once took that matter up with the Railway Commission. My hon. friend from Edmonton says that he protests here and now. I say to him: Why did you not protest then and there for the fifteen years when you sat with your friends on this side of the House? I do say that this 'protesting here and now' comes with ill grace from men who, for ten years, for twelve years, for fifteen years, remained in power and offered no solution for the transportation problem except the creation of new roads built with increased fixed charges that are hung a3 a millstone around the neck of the farmers of western Canada for

_ali time to come are to be met. And this is clear to any man who will analyse these figures. I would ask my hon. friend from Carleton to go to the library and consult the latest issue of Poor's Railway Manual and compare this new with other roads, and see whether we in western Canada have been honestly and fairly dealt with in the enormous charges placed upon us for all time in connection with the last-named road.

House in Committee on Bill No. 176, respecting the Southampton Railway Company.-Mr. Crocket.
On section 1-declaration:

We had to reconstruct this Bill, in order to do in the usual way, instead of in an unusual and doubtful way, what was desired to be done. There is in New Brunswick a provincial road thirteen miles in length which has been assisted by the province to the extent of $12,000 a mile, andthe Canadian Pacific railway obtained the right to use this road for ninety-nine years. The provincial government have consented as guardians or trustees of the people in regard to the provincial road just as we ar*



the custodians oi the peoples' rights in regard to Dominion charters. They gave consent on behalf of the lessees. It was necessary that the Dominion Parliament should, consent in the case of the Canadian Pacific railway, the Dominion creature. That has been done in the usual way. The Senate declared the road to be for the general advantage of Canada, taking it from provincial jurisdiction simply because it wanted to lease to a Dominion road. What we have done is to recommend that the title of the Bill shall be'changed on the third reading to 'An Act respecting the Southampton Railway Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.' We have changed the preamble to set forth the *acts as they are:
That whereas the Southampton Railway Company has by its petition represented that it was incorporated by chapter 46 of the statutes of 1910 of the province of New Brunswick, and that by chapter 12 of the statutes of 1911 of New Brunswick it was authorized to enter into an agreement and lease with the Canadian Pacific railway, hereinafter called the company, as herein provided.
We struck out the clause making the declaration that it should be a woTk for the general advantage of Canada. We have the usual amalgamation clause but we specifically mention what the amalgamation is to be.

I think that is satisfactory. There are disputes regarding rights of way and I was wondering if the effect of declaring this to- be a work for the general advantage of Canada would be to bring it under Dominion jurisdiction and possibly affect existing litigation.
That is one thing we had in view in the changes that were made.
