House resumed consideration of the proposed motion of Mr. Martin, that the House do now adjourn.

At six o'clock I had drawn attention to the fact that the first factoT to be considered in fixing a freight-rate was the fixed charges that had to be borne to enable a railway company to meet its obligations on its securities. I pointed out what these charges were in respect to the three great roads in western Canada. I had pointed out it when I Mr. LANCASTER
first went West, fifteen years ago, we had only one road. At present we have three and I would ask any gentleman opposite to point out a single instance in which there has been any reduction in freight rates by reason of their transportation policy. I say that that is an important and serious thing for the people to consider and when gentlemen come here to oppose and criticise the first effort that has been made to have the tribunal created by law seriously consider the whole question, I ask them whether they can point to a single reduction that was made in the burden of freight rates cast on the people of the West, during the fifteen years they were in power.
There is, however, an outstanding case in which rates in western Canada have been reduced. The Government of Manitoba took over the Northern Pacific lines, and subsequently leased them to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. By reason of their taking over these lines they reduced the freight rates on grain by a very substantial sum and also reduced the rates on general commodities twenty-five per cent. That reduction had a direct effect upon the freight rate policy of the other roads in western Canada, and the Canadian Pacific railway, long before there was what I might call any efficient competition from other lines, made certain reductions by reason of the policy of the Manitoba Government. These are the facts which may be ascertained from the records, and about which there can be no real dispute. We had the new provinces created, and they commenced to guarantee the securities of branch lines. Unlike the province of Manitoba, the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta not only guarantee the securities of the branch lines for the roads I have mentioned, some of them operating under provincial charters, and some of them under federal charters, but in the province of Alberta, and in one instance at least in the province of Saskatchewan, they exempted those lines from ail forms of taxation for the whole period of the guarantee, and made no bargain of any kind, shape or description, as to the rates that might be charged by those lines for transportation.
To what line in Saskatchewan does my hon. friend refer ?
The Grand Trunk Pacific branch lines.

That is not so. Not a
branch of the Grand Trunk Pacific is exempted.
The Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk railway both did it. Now they are not exempt in Saskatchewan for the whole, but in AlbeTta they are still exempt for the whole period of guarantee.

I know nothing about
Alberta.

My hon. friend knows
what the facts are in Saskatchewan. I have pointed out what they were originally in that province and what they are now. It is true that they saw the error of their ways, so far as that is concerned, but my hon. friend does not assert and cannot assert that they made any condition as to the amount of rates that should be charged.
For the very good reason that they cannot.

Heretofore I have had
a fair regard for the legal acumen of the hon. gentleman, but when he says that they cannot, he either says something which he knows to be absolutely incorrect, or he is more ignorant than I thought he was. Either horn of the dilemma is sufficient for my purpose. The province of British Columbia legislating after the legislatures of Alberta and Saskatchewan, did make a binding contract for control of rates that ousted the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, the branch lines that were guaranteed, as my hon. friend should know, held local charters over which the local legislature had supreme and complete control until such time as they were brought under federal control and obtained federal charters. He should know that. We have the province of Manitoba with control over its freight rates by reason of the agreement made with the Canadian Northern Railway Company. We have the province of Saskatchewan without control, and we have the province of Alberta without control, and in addition the railways being exempted from taxation for the whole period of the guarantee. In addition to that, we have the province of Manitoba taking two per cent of the gross,earnings for taxation, while in Saskatchewan the sum now fixed is merely a nominal one per mile, that is according to the statutes, at least-my hon. friend from Regina may have different information as to that. These are the facts. This Government came into power with these facts before them, and the first thing they did was to refer the matter to the tribunal created by law for that purpose, and that tribunal heard evidence. It is perfectly true that the first thing the late chairman of that board did was to hold that the onus was on the railway companies to show that their rates were not an undue preference or an unjust discrimination. Judging from the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin)	and the hon. member for
Edmonton (Mr. Oliver)-the hon. member 284i
for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) did seem to realize that it was a judicial matter-the debate has proceeded this afternoon upon an entirely erroneous conception of the statute. Either my hon. friend from Edmonton did not read the statute, or he did not want to read it. I repeat that these are the facts. Then the matter came before the Board of Railway Commissioners, and that board ruled that the onus was on the railway companies to establish that was not undue preference or unjust discrimination in the rates. Here is the section of the Act which I will read. My hon. friend from Regina in my judgment attempted to make it appear that what the Railway Commission was doing now was something that was not authorized by the statute, and the hon. member for Edmonton who followed stated that the railways were violating the statutes and should be brought to ask for doing so. For ten years he was not much concerned about that, but it has suddenly struck him that it would be a nice thing to be concerned about it. It is another case of here and now, instead of there and then. Here is the section:
Whenever it is shown that any company charges one person, company, or class of persons, or the persons in any district, lower tolls for the same or similar goods, or lower tolls for the same or similar eeir vices, than it charges to other persons, companies, or classes of persons, or to the persons in another district, or makes any difference in treatment in respect of such companies or persons, the burden of proving that such lower toll oir difference in treatment, does not amount to an undue preference or an unjust discrimination shall lie on the company.
It is not any difference in tolls that gives that board jurisdiction, it is not discrimination, it is not a change in tolls; it must be an undue preference, or an unjust discrimination. My hon. friend from Regina has surely overlooked that it must be an undue preference or an unjust discrimination. The learned chairman of the board said that the onus was on the companies to establish their case. He said:	I rule that these rates are undue
and unjust. Then what was. the further matter at issue? The additional matter at issue became the reasonableness of the tolls as a whole, and the question which the Board of Railway Commissioners is today considering is not only the question ot unjust discrimination or undue preference, it is the question of whether or not the rates charged in western Canada bear any proportion to the service rendered by the transportation companies. That is the problem now being considered. Then what happened? There were adjournments as my hon. friend from Regina read from the record. Had he read a line or two further down he would have found that it was counsel for the provinces of Saskat-

chewan and Alberta who made the application for the long adjournment. Here are the words which appear in the manuscript of my hon. friend (Mr. Martin):
The next meeting was held by the hoard on October 7, when the railway companies endeavoured to justify the onus of proof which had been cast upon them on the 16th day of April.	.... Mr. Cowan
stated that in view of his other engagements and the immense mass of statistics to he digested that he could not proceed on the date named by the Chief Commissioner-November 4. However, owing to representations made by Mr. Cowan the meeting was subsequently postponed to January 7, 1913.
Whose counsel was Mr. Cowan?

He was counsel for the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and this is what I find on page 11 of my hon. friend's manuscript:
Mr. Cowan had no assistance in fighting for this apparently long adjournment. The counsel for the Dominion Government had not even intimated that they were not prepared and ready to go on on the 4th of November, and after the Chief Commissioner had suggested the 4th of November, he asked Mr.-Whitla at page 9975:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
What do you say, Mr. Whitla?
Mr. Whitla: Mr. Chairman, as far as counsel for the Dominion Government is concerned we are largely in the hands of the board. This is one branch of the case, discrimination only.
The Chief Commissioner: I think it is every branch of the case, discrimination and everything.
What then is the position? We find that the meetings were held and evidence was taken, and the case was adjourned six or seven weeks ago for the purpose of enabling a mass of statistics to be put in by the railway companies in answer to the parole evidence and statistics submitted by the Dominion and by the provinces. My hon. friend says, why go to the United States to get evidence? He knows as well as any man living, as was said by my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) that you cannot possibly get disinterested evidence unless you go to someone who is disinterested, and in the Dominion the three great railroads were all represented by counsel before that board. I wish to point out to this House what is the serious feature of this whole case, as it is a matter which sooner or later must be brought to the attention of the House, that is the statement that was made by Mr. Hanna on behalf of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and by a representative of the Grand Trunk Pacific that if the railways were pressed to the point urged by counsel it would be impossible for these railways to carry on Mr. BENNETT (Calgary).
their business, having regard to the magnitude of their fixed charges and the cost of operation.
These are statements made before the tribunal and supported by statistics. Is it not a matter of supreme concern to the people of this country that such a question should be carefully considered; is it a light matter for a tribunal charged with that grave responsibility, to say: we will, by one stroke of the pen, cut down the rates of all these transportion companies ? And, if the evidence produced by the Canadian Northern and by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Companies be correct, then the solvency of these two companies is threatened, and their ability to pay the fixed charges put upon them by this Parliament is jeopardized. That is the seriousness of the position.
When the hon. gentleman from Regina (Mr. Martin) attempts to make political capital out of this, I would have him understand that not only the credit of the railways but the credit of Canada is at issue, because anything that injuriously affects the welfare of these two great railway companies is detrimental to the welfare of the whole Dominion. If, as I said, the statements made on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and the Canadian Northern Company are correct, then the guarantees of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta might have to become effective and what would the hon. gentleman from Regina think of that? The hon. gentleman told us that he did not come here to criticise the Board of Railway Commissioners, but he did come to criticise the Government, and with a longing that is ever present in his mind to gain some little publicity by an attack on this Government which is endeavouring to do something for.this country and to do it honestly and well, he cheerfully launched out in his unfounded criticism. But, the criticism of the hon. gentleman is really directed against the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. And why? The very first section of the Act creating that tribunal declares it is a court of record, and the hon. member stands here while this case is subjudice, and he condems that Board for having granted an adjournment. Is that his idea of professional etiquette; is it his idea of the duty of counsel to criticise a court and to endeavour to prejudice it in the eyes of the country? And all that he is able to charge against the Board of Railway Commissioners is that it granted an adjournment, which was urged in the first instance by counsel for the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. When that court of record, constituted by statute, did grant the adjournment, counsel for this Government stood in his place as was his duty and said:

I am in the hands of the court. The hon. member condemns counsel for that. The adjournment was granted, not at the instance of the federal Government, and not at the instance of the counsel who represented the people and who are so sneeringly referred to by the hon. member for Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell). Let me tell him that the gentlemen who represent the Dominion of Canada before the tribunal in this case have forgotten more law than he ever knew or than he ever will know. Let me tell the hon. member for Regina that it ill becomes a young man like him to speak in such sneering terms about the qualifications of the legal gentlemen who represent the people of Canada in that case; let me tell him further that the counsel for the Dominion are gentlemen quite equal in their profession to the gentleman who represents the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. I am not saying much when I say that. When it comes to a question of law, no one would accuse that gentleman of being a profound lawyer. A profound knowledge of the fundamental principles upon which railway freight rates are based, is as foreign to him as it is to the hon. gentleman himself. A more complex, intricate and difficult problem never engaged the attention of any tribunal than this question of the adjustment of freight rates in western Canada. The gentlemen who are charged with the responsibility of adjusting these rates have a duty not only to western Canada but to the'people of the whole country, because every part of Canada must be affected by their judgment. More than that, the credit of the country itself is affected.
The hon. gentleman from Regina (Mr. Martin) has come into this high court of Parliament, while a case was still under consideration by the Court created by this Parliament; while the evidence is incomplete, while the witnesses are still to be called, while the arguments of counsel had not been made, and he has stated that be-that court granted an adjournment that was asked for in the first instance by counsel for the provinces, whom he lauds so highly, in order that his other engagements might be kept, the Government of Canada is guilty of laches in not prosecuting the case. This is the first reflection I have heard in this country upon the bona fides of any judicial tribunal, and, Sir, there is no doubt in the world that his attack upon the Railway Commission, is as wholly unwarranted as it is possible -for anything to be unwarranted. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) said he had the highest opinion of the Railway Board, and he added that during all the time he occupied a'seat in this House, he never heard a Conservative member make the slightest criticism of that tribunal. He is right. It is not the habit of the members of the Conservative party With whom I am associated to cast reflections upon ti,e judiciary of the land, ho matter how strong in some instances the temptation may be.. It is an attribute of the Conservative party in this country to show respect for our constituted judicial tribunals, and I would commend our example in that respect to some of the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. As a matter of fact the Government had had no more to do with the adjournment granted by the Board of Railway Commissioners than has the hon. gentleman himself. I would point out to the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) that if he is so particularly anxious about the vindication of the law in this case it is perfectly open to him, and it has been open to him for the last eight years, to go down to the Board of Railway Commissioners and put in motion himself the machinery that will enable the case to be proceeded with. The procedure before that tribunal allows him to do that, but I have not heard of him having done it. But this afternoon, dealing with a large problem affecting the well-being of the entire community, the hon. gentleman made a vicious attack upon the Minister of Railways, who since he assumed the portfolio has engaged himself day and night in the conscientious discharge of his duties, and who is not the official joker to the Administration, as some Ministers of Railways have been. No man knows better than the hon. member for Regina that the Minister of Railways has made an honest effort to solve this problem, and no man knows better than he that if any undue delay has occurred it is not the Government that is responsible. The hon. member knows all this but in order to make a little political capital for himself, and in the* hope that tomorrow morning his name will be extended in big type across the Liberal newspapers in the West, and that the Regina Leader will tell how he fought for the rights of the West, struggled for the down-trodden farmers of the plains against the great octopus which is crushing out the lives of the farmers of the West-
Do not look so angry.
The Canadian Pacific railway is all right, do not worry.

I am glad my hon.
friend from Edmonton has mentioned that, although he will probably be unable to appreciate the fact that I am one man in this House who is $10,000 a year poorer because I severed my connection with the Canadian Pacific railway. I will admit that the hon. member for Edmonton cannot understand any man doing that.

Not the member for
Calgary.

8980

Oh, well, I do not
remember of any photograph having appeared in any newspaper of a document with reference to any sums of money 1
have received. I merely mention that in passing.
These are the broad facts of the case and they speak for themselves. My hon. friend from Regina cannot contradict them; they cannot be contradicted. Let me tell him that discrimination does not give you a case before the Board of Railway Commissioners. The rates from Toronto to Sudbury and the Soo are the same, but that does not give you a case; the rates between Fort William, Calgary and Edmonton, are the same, but that does not give you a case although the mileage is entirely different. Your claim must be based upon something other than that, 'but I hesitate to discuss the case because it is now before the board. I would hate to think for a single moment that the Board of Railway Commissioners gave a decision upon this case that would open up three weeks or a month or six months from now the whole matter again. It must be based upon law and accurate knowledge. Let me give my hon. friend a case. I happened to be in Spokane when the case of the Northern Pacific and the Great Northern was being heard. That case was started nearly twenty years ago before the Inter-State Commerce Commission. What was the point? The point at issue was as to whether or not the charge made by a railway company for the carriage of traffic to the coast-that is to the sea- could be less than the pro rata charge made to an inland town like Spokane. The Board of Trade and the Chamber of Commerce at Spokane fought that matter during all the intervening years, beaten today, victorious to-morrow, then beaten again, until finally about three years ago they got a judgment in their favour. What happened? The case was re-heard; and even to-day, despite that long struggle, no order has been made effective to reduce the freight rates to Spokane and to place them upon the basis for which they were contending.

Does- the hon. member
hold that out as a precedent for this country?

No, but the Supreme
Court of the United States held that the rates charged to terminii could not be applied to inland towns.
We, in Calgary, Edmonton and Regina, have endeavoured from time to time to invoke the aid of that Spokane case in order to have rates charged from the Atlantic seaboard to Calgary, Edmonton and Regina made pro rata to the traffic rates to the Pacific seaboard, but we have been unable to do it. The Supreme Court of the United Mr. BENNETT (Calgary*
States has upheld the contention that the rate for through traffic does not bear any pro rata relation to the rate to intervening points.

Does the hon. member
mean to argue that the Railway Commission would not have power to decide the matter the other way?
I have no doubt about the fact that the Railway Commission would have power to fix any rates at all.
Where does the application come in?

The question as to
what should be a reasonable rate is also now before the tribunal. There must be a rate fixed having regard to the fixed charges, the physical conditions of the country and all the surrounding circumstances, the density of the traffic and so on. My hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin) was entirely wrong in his statement about that. When he spoke about the density of traffic, he spoke about something that was alleged in the prima facie case established by the records of the Vancouver case. The companies in determining the density of traffic included in their figures the traffic of Manitoba for instance as being not only Manitoba traffic proper but all the traffic of Alberta and Saskatchewan that passed through that province as well as that of British Columbia. When the matter was heard and the railway companies in their answer in rebuttal, they destroyed that entirely. The facts which were summarized by my friend from Regina this afternoon are the facts of this prima facie case before the evidence had been heard at all. As to whether or not the prima facie case has been entirely destroyed must rest with the judgfes just as a prima facie case must be considered in the light of the evidence given by and for the defendant. I trust I make myself clear upon that point. One of the very great difficulties under; which we laboured was apparently a false conception as to our statistics, because we had regarded the prima facie case as being based upon a correct statement, whereas in fact it was based upon all the traffic from all the provinces, having regard to the density of traffic in the country through which it passed to reach Fort William. When it comes down to a question of relative rates, my hon. friend from Regina knows that the freight tolls per mile in Canada are about three-quarters of a cent per ton per mile. That is something less than the sum earned by most of the railways traversing the same kind of territory in the United States. That is part of the answer put in by the Railway companies. I hope my friend has read

it, because it is extremely interesting and at the same time difficult reading. What has to be considered is whether or not the commission is able from the evidence that is produced before it and the evidence given by the statistics to conclude first, that there has been an undue preference between the East and the West, that is that western freight rates have been raised unduly in comparison with those in the East and whether there has been undue discrimination between the East and the West at the expense of the West. If that is not established, there further remains the question as to the reasonableness of the freight rates. All these matters are matters which must be determined by that court, and I submit that it is unfair to ask this Parliament to endeavour to prejudge that case or to blame the judges for doing the best they can with a most difficult case. If it took the Inter-State Commerce Commission in Spokane years and years to deal with that great problem, is it fair to say that, because this case has not made rapid enough progress, this Parliament must criticise and censure the men who. are endeavouring to do their duty. That is what this motion is and it is most unfair.
I have heard a good deal this afternoon as to the intolerable burden that is being borne by the people of the West in connection with freight rates. My hon. friend from Edmonton has referred to the fact that it is my business to know something of freight rates. He cannot understand that it is no longer my business. I have endeavoured to profit from the knowledge I learned. For several years it was my business to know something of freight rates There is a burden borne by the farmers of the West that is even worse than freight rates. I suppose it has not crossed the 'mind of the average member to ask himself how much of this burden that is borne 'by the people of the West is really because of the freight rates and how much because of something else. I should like to tell my hon. friends that bad roads cost the farmers of the West more than excessive freight rates. As my friends may question that, let me prove it. It has been absolutely and conclusively demonstrated that, owing to the nature of the soil and the bad roads which we have in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, the farmers are able to haul to the market only something like forty bushels of grain per load and that the average distance that the farmers are from the elevators and railroads at the present time is between fifteen and twenty miles. That sounds like a very small load. Given good roads in a dry season, they are able to haul from eighty to a hundred bushels of grain to the market. I have interviewed the farmers and have obtained that information from them. If the
farmer's time is worth anything at all, and if his team is worth anything, it means that it had cost him all the way from ten to fifteen cents a bushel to haul his grain from the farm to the elevator. The freight charges from the elevator to Fort William are in many instances no greater than that. In one instance that came under my notice, the sum charged to transport the wheat from the railway elevator to Liverpool was less than the sum it cost the farmer to haul it. from his field to the elevator. That is then the real burden interfering with the farmers getting the profits they should from their husbandry? The excessive charge that is made upon them to get 'their crop to the railways in the first instance varies from ten to fifteen cents a bushel. The other evening h-on. gentlemen opposite were content to put themselves on record as opposed to the only effort I have seen in Canada to provide a general system of highways. That is the reason the West is so vitally interested in a matter of that character.
It has been said that we should discuss this matter without any party spirit. Did hon. gentlemen opposite make their observations in a non-partisan spirit? The hon. member for Red Deer attacked the Government for not reducing freight rates. But the hon. member for Carleton said, very properly, that this matter was in the hands of a court. The hon. member for Edmonton shows no spirit of partisanship-none whatever-that is, not more than usual. The hon. member for Regina, as I said, in his desire to obtain publicity, showed just that party spirit that always characterizes his utterances. The hon. member for Medicine Hat, I must say, did seem to desire to say something free from party animus. I have looked over the Votes and Proceedings of this House, for a good many years, and I cannot remember having ever seen the names of these hon. gentlemen who appealed for a lack of party spirit recorded as voting in a way that would indicate that they had any mind or opinions beyond that mind and those opinions that might be given to them by those who directed their destinies. Especially is this true of the hon. member for Red Deer, who vaunts his independence outdoors, but in this House, votes yea or nay as he is told..
Now, so far as the facts in this case are concerned, I have indicated in a general way what they are, and I say frankly that those facts cannot be controverted or contradicted. I do not propose to constitute myself a court of appeal for the purpose of determining the justice of the case that is endeavoured to be made by the people of the West, because I believe it serves no good purpose to the farmers on the western plains to merely say that they are suffering rfom exeesive rates still less to endeavour to 'censure a court 'before it has given its opiu

89?4
ion, to pre-judge a case that has not been heard, to sit in the seat of the scornful as did my horn friend from Regina, without hearkening to the witnesses, without waiting for the addresses of counsel, but endeavouring to constitute himself a judge in Israel, lest some benefit might come to the Government that has instituted this inquiry which, I believe, will he of untold benefit to the people of western Canada.

I have listened to my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) with a great deal of care; and I should have listened with greater pleasure had there not been introduced into his remarks a spirit of partisanship, a venom, if I may use the expression, which was not called for. It may be that the hon. gentleman cannot address the House in any other manner. The effort has been made to represent the course taken by hon. members on this side with reference to this question as one of condemnation of a court created by this Parliament, this being the result of partisan spirit. Of course, no one would ever eharge my hon. friend from Calgary with having any party venom in his make-up; and yet they could hardly iisten even to the remarks he uttered in closing his address to-day without concluding that he and other hon. gentlemen opposite were most interested in dealing with this matter from a persona] and political standpoint instead of from the standpoint of conditions which have prevailed in western Canada. I have been in this House a good many years, and I am bound to say that the subject under discussion this afternoon is one that has been very prolific of debate in the past. Never has there been a year during the time T have had the honour of a seat in this House when this subject has not been presented in one form or another, not merely once but on many occasions during a session. This time the matter has been presented, and I think very ably presented, by my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin). It certainly was presented in a calm and deliberative way, and the hon. gentleman's position was sustained by facts which prove his case clearly up to the hilt. That case my hon. friend who has just taken his seat has not attempted to answer.
I was very much amused at the hon. member for Calgary when he turned from the question of the railway grievances on account of freight rates to the conditions prevailing in western Canada as respects highways. He argued in effect that because the farmers are under a heavy burden by reason of the condition of their highways, due to the soil and other conditions and to the fact that they have no turnpike roads, because they are suffering disadvantages in this way, therefore this.
Mr. BENNETT 'Calagry).
Parliament is not interested in considering the question as to the disadvantages under which they labour in connection with the freight rates-that because they are burdened with heavy costs in transportation from their farms to the railway stations therefore they should be burdened with heavy freight rates to the markets which they are seeking with their products.
The hon. gentleman says that the fact that you consider this matter and deal with it in the way it has been dealt with this afternoon means that you are attacking the tribunal, you Are dealing with a case that is sub judice, that befere the case is determined you are dealing with the court. Not so, Mr. Speaker. The Railway Board, a very excellent tribunal and a very successful one, was the creation of this Parliament. We delegated to them certain authority and certain powers, and in so delegating that authority we have a right to see that they exercise it. My hon. friend from Regina has shown that this matter has not been properly and satisfactorily dealt with by that board. He has shown the grievance under which the farmers and the public of western Canada labour, and he has pointed out that there have been delays that are unwarranted. My hon. friend from Calgary has said: Oh, but the representative of the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta asked for an adjournment from November until the 7th of January. Did that representa^ tive ask on behalf of the provinces for inaction from January 7 down to the present time? It may be that when the evidence was put in before the tribunal that representative wished to study, and so asked for an adjournment. But he did not ask it for a longer time than the 7th of January. And even though there is justification for the Railway Board not dealing with the case promptly before January last, certainly that is no justification for the delay that has resulted since that date.
I think we do not always bear in mind what has occurred. Away back in the years that have gone, this subject has been a matter of general complaint by almost every member coming from western Canada, whether he sat to the right or to the left of the Speaker, and many theories have been advanced as to the causes of the discrimination which has existed. Admittedly there have been very excessive railway freight rates in western Canada, and admittedly there has been discrimination against the West in favour of the East. We have on many occasions in the past gone into the causes of these conditions as they exist, and I do not intend to do so at this time. It has been truly said by many members from western Canada that this condition originated away back at the time of the con-

struction of the Canadian Pacific railway, and that it was due to the monopoly that was granted to that railway at the time of its inception and construction. I do not . propose to discuss that feature of the matter, nor to go into the merits of the action taken with respect to that monopoly. In any case, that monopoly did exist, whether justified or not. It may have been a very logical result of the conditions which prevailed in those years, and it may have been the only solution to what was admittedly a very serious problem.
The hon. member for Calgary has referred to the fact that the Mackenzie Administration sought to have the Canadian Pacific railway constructed at an even greater price than was subsequently paid. He might have gone further and said that the Government of Canada turned away from the construction of the road as a government work and sought to find a company to take hold of it. That was in the early seventies, and later on another government was successful in securing a company to take hold of the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway, and they successfully put it through. It has been! claimed that this was done at very great expense to the country. Admitting that it was, it might with equal candor be said that it was justified by reason of the existing conditions. I have heard hon. members say on the floor of this House that the construction of that road, in the construction of portions of the railway that were handed over to the Canadian Pacific1 railway corporation, in the land grants and in the money subsidies, cost the people of this country about $400,000,000. They have argued that on the floor of this House, to their own satisfaction at least, but it is immaterial in the discussion of this question whether the road cost $400,000,000 or whether it cost less or even more. We must all admit that there was given to this company at the time of the construction of the road, a complete control of the freight rates that they should impose upon the traffic of western Canada. They did exercise their rights in that regard, and for many years they were not subject to any control. They were exempt from the control of the Government, and afterwards when the Railway Board was created, they for many years stood aloof and refused to be subject to its juris-[DOT] diction.
The hon. member for Calgary has repeated his usual argument, that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House were for fifteen years entrusted with the government of this country, and during that period they were inactive in this regard and did nothing. Even if they were, that was no answer to the charges brought to the attention of this House by the hon. member for Regina this afternoon. The
question of freight rates on the Canadian Pacific railway could not be dealt with by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council previous to the coming into force of the Railway Act of 1903; no attempt was ever made by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council to deal with or to regulate freight rates on the different lines of railway throughout Canada. In 1903 the Liberal Government of that day created a board and gave them power to regulate and control the freight rates not only of eastern Canada but in western Canada as well. As 1 have said, the Canadian Pacific railway stood aloof and declined to come within the jurisdiction of that board. When the Crow's Nest Pass contract between the Government of Canada and the Canadian Pacific railway was entered into, one of the considerations was that there should be a reduction of freight rates on western traffic in connection with the Canadian Pacific railway. Up to that time and for some years afterwards there was no competition with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in western Canada, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, under pressure brought to bear by the Laurier Administration at the time of the construction of the Crow's Nest Pass railway, revolutionized, I might almost say, their freight tariff, or, at least, moderated and lowered it, to the advantage and benefit of the people who were interested in western traffic. Subsequently, when these other railways, the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific, to which my hon. friend has referred, began to loom on the horizon as competitors, then it was that the Canadian Pacific railway voluntarily came forward and said:	We will
submit to the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission; we will place ourselves on a parity with the other railway companies of Canada in that regard, and we will graciously permit the Railway Commission of Canada to regulate our freight tariff in connection with their regulation of other freight tariffs. They did that, as I say, as a matter of grace; but there is not to be found on the statute books of this country any enactment which compels them to submit to the orders and decrees of the Railway Commission. A Bill was introduced this session by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), relating to this very subject, but it is buried in the morgue of troublesome legislation-under public Bills and orders, where it is to be found as No. 36. It cannot be resurrected and cannot be dealt with. The company have not brought legislation binding themselves to submit to the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. The Government has not brought in any Bill imposing that legal obligation upon them. A private member brings in such a Bill and that private mem-

ber under the rules of the House, must be shut out from forcing that measure through so that the Canadian Pacific railway would stand on an equal footing with other railway corporations in Canada in relation to the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission over it.
My hon. friend said that there has been fifteen years of inactivity. There is to the credit of the party now sitting on this side of the House, first the action taken with respect to the Crow's Nest agreement in securing from the Canadian Pacific railway a lessening of freight rates. There is the action of that party in 1903 in the enactment of the Railway Act and the creation of a Railway Commission regulating the railways of the country and having entire jurisdiction with respect to the tolls and tariffs which railways might charge on freight and passengers. Then they constructed the Grand Trunk Pacific and aided the construction of the Canadian Northern railway. I shall not stop to say how that aid was given, but both of these railways were assisted and created to provide additional railway facilities and incidentally competition through the West in the matter of railway facilities. The very moment that was done the Canadian Pacific railway was forced or atleast persuaded to come within the jurisdiction of the board which regulates the freight tariff of the country. But my hon. friend from Calgary, by a strange method of logic, says that to the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific is due in a very large measure, if not wholly, the difficulties and the grievances in regard to excessive freight rates in western Canada; and by a peculiar process of reasoning he says that freight rates must be controlled and governed by what he is pleased to term fixed charges. He has said that the Canadian Northern railway fixed charges were $1,000 per mile and the Grand Trunk fixed charges were about $2,000 per mile. T shalf deal with the principle that should govern and be taken into consideration in the matter of determining the reasonableness of freight rates but when my hon. friend goes to that extreme and charges the complaints of the West to the construction by the Laurier Government of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, it seems to me that he is driven into a very small corner indeed. Let me say that while the fixed charges are a factor in the matter of regulating the reasonableness of freight Tates they are not by any means the controlling factor, in fact, Sir, they are a very small and insignificant feature in the determining of that reasonableness and for obvious reasons. A railway may be constructed in the most flimsy manner, as was the Canadian Pacific railway, admittedly, originally, with its wooden trestles, with its very imperfect Mr. EMMERSON
ballasting, with its want of permanency, built for the moment and to meet a contingency.
I am not complaining of the course taken. In doing that they were, I believe, serving the best interests not only of themseves but of the country. In so doing they determined what is known as the fixed charges. But the governing charges are the cost of operation and transporting the traffic over the line. The less permanent a line of railway is, the less perfect it is, the less money invested in its roadbed and in its rolling stock, the greater in proportion is the cost of maintenance and operation. My hon. friend has perhaps a certain object in view in calling attention to the fixed charges of the Grand Trunk Pacific and placing them at $2,000 and the Canadian Pacific railway fixed charges at $800 per mile. The Canadian Pacific railway may represent $800 per mile for its fixed charges originally but we all recognize that the Canadian Pacific railway up to date, the transcontinental line known as the Canadian Pacific railway across this continent to-day, is an entirely different railway from the Canadian Pacific railway as it was when it was first opened to traffic in the early eighties. Why the change? It certainly has cost money. Where wooden trestles were you will find heavy fills.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member is taking great latitude in this debate. The definite matter of urgent importance handed to me is that the investigation of western freight rates now pending before the Railway Commission should be proceeded with at once. That is a defined matter. There is, of course, a bearing when you come to show the different fixed charges, and what elements might enter into the determination of freight rates, as it might or might not cause delay in the investigation. I think that would be pertinent; but the history of these railways beyond that would not be permissible on this definite matter.

You will admit that
the hon. member for Calgary went into the question of the cost of those two railways and made a comparison and I am simply answering him. I claim the privilege of following him.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I felt more than once
that I should call attention to it, but I felt that he was dealing with the history of these railways and showing that, on account of that it required a much longer time for the commission to deal with the freight rates having to do with these inquiries. That is, to my mind, directly applicable to the subject.

I did not understand that he was putting the case in that way,

but in an entirely different way and he
sought to make it a political question. I am following the trail that was blazed by my hon. friend. It would seem to be only fair that I should be permitted to follow that line, and I shall reach a conclusion in the relevancy of which I think, you, Sir, will concur.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have watched the debate very closely, and I have felt disposed several times to interfere. It must be understood that it is with great reluctance that the Speaker interferes in such discussions. In so far as references were made to show the impossibility of bringing to a rapid termination the question under consideration by the Railway Commission, I think they were applicable to the case; but when an hon. member goes into the history of the Crow's Nest railway and other road3, it seems to me that he is taking rather a wide latitude in a matter of definite specific and urgent importance.

It is of importance
that this matter should be dealt with promptly, and I was just coming to the point raised by-my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett). He spoke of the fixed charges. Now the reason why the Canadian Pacific railway fixed charges are put at 800 is because the road has been changed in character. They have been taken out of the earnings of the road. Therefore the fixed charges do not appear in proportion to the fixed charges of the other roads. The Grand Trunk Pacific was made a permanent road, with stone and steel culverts, and its grades of an entirely different character from that of the grades on the Canadian Pacific railway. My hon. friend can take this consolation that away back in 1879 and 1880 and 1881, the Government and the people of Canada treated the Canadian Pacific railway so generously, contributed to their coffers so freely, and gave them such immense blocks of land that the Canadian Pacific railway has been able to wrest and wring from the pockets of the people of Canada sufficient not only to pay handsome dividends but to have a surplus of earnings enabling it to change the whole character of the road and to make it permanent, so that the fixed charges, so called, would not bear against them in the way it was anticipated. That is a relevant point it seems to me.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I confess that it does
not appear so to me. The question as to the fixed charges of those roads, however they may have been brought about, and whether high or low, does not seem to me a matter of any importance. The question of how the Railway Commission should obtain information in order to reach a proper conclusibn as to the fixed charges, is relevant, but how the fixed charges
came to be made, does not seem to me of special importance in this discussion.

My hon. friend from Calgary made a charge that the party on this side of the House had done nothing for fifteen years and were doing nothing to remedy the situation. I have attempted to show that when the late Government was charged with responsibility, and since they have sat in Opposition their attitude has been to insist upon these grievances being remedied by this commission, and promptly. At the last session of this Parliament a resolution was introduced in this House by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways proposing to grant a subsidy of $12,000 per mile to a railway company in British Columbia, and the Liberal Opposition in this House sought to make it a condition precedent of the granting of the subsidy to have the railway which was to be thus aided submit to the, jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. But the Government declined to impose that condition, and granted the subsidy.
My hon. friend from Calgary has referred to the attitude of the Saskatchewan Government and of the Alberta Government. While I thought that that had nothing to do with the question before the House, it seemed to me that in view of the course he had taken, it was proper for me to show the other side of the shield, and to show the responsibility of this Government, without in any way attempting to deal with the responsibility of the governments of the prairie provinces. They may have been derelict in their duty, but is that an answer to the charge that may be brought against this Government of dereliction of duty? There was another case, that of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, in which it was proposed to grant a large subsidy to the Government of Ontario not merely in aid of the construction of that road, but to recoup the Government of Ontario for the money expended on it. At the last session of this House the Liberal Opposition proposed that that railway should come under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission, but that also was opposed by the present Government. This Government are responsible for the conditions which prevail in connection with the freight rates in the West, so far as they have existed during the past two years. It is not necessary for me to attempt to make any excuses for conditions which prevailed under the former Government, though it may be a matter of satisfaction to my hon. friend from Calgary to make statements which cannot be supported, and which have been refuted by me already in the instances to which I have called your attention. I hold that the matter of the reasonableness of freight rates on railways in Canada, as well as on railways anywhere on the face of the globe

is not wholly, or even measureably, based on fixed charges. It must be based upon the cost of operation and the cost of maintenance of the road, upon the cost of transporting traffic over rails of tlhat road. These are the governing features, and in that cost the gradients are a governing feature. The curvature of the line is not less important. The actual cost of transportation of traffic over any railway in Canada can be demonstrated to a mathematical certainty. The Intercolonial has that cost brought down to a certainty every year, and there is not a railway in Canada that, does not do it.
This important question, as to whether the freight rates in western Canada are on a reasonable basis, and whether they are or are not discriminatory as against the West, should be adjudicated on without interminable delay. On the 7th of January last the Minister of Railways was clothed with power to tell the Railway Commission that this matter must be attended to, but he has not shown that he has taken action, nor has he shown that his counsel has made any attempt to expedite the decision of the board. Whether the Liberals or the Conservatives are responsible for the conditions that prevail in western Canada.
I shall net inquire, but I do say that this has been a burning question almost ever since the beginning -of the operation of the Canadian Pacific railway, and admittedly there are grievances in the West which call for a remedy. The tariffs of the railway companies are operative, so long as no exception is taken to them by the board, and it is obvious that if the decision of the commission can be deferred, benefit will accrue to the Tailway companies to the detriment of the people of the West. The admitted delays in this matter, even since the 7th of January last are inexcusable and indefensible, and the Government apparently is responsible. Apparently at every hearing counsel for the Government is reconciled to delay; the board itself has not been exercising that diligence it was its duty to exercise, and the people continue to suffer. The hon. member for Regina has wisely brought this matter to the attention of the House and of the country, and if the Minister of Railways even now exercises diligence, I have no doubt that before ten days it can be dealt with.
We are told that a traffic expert has to be obtained from the United States, but I think everyone will admit that the traffic experts of the Government railways of Canada would be disinterested as between the public and the railway companies. That being so, there is no necessity for bringing an expert from the United States. The Government could have gone to Mr. Tiffin, traffic manager of the Inter-Mr. EMMERSON
colonial railway; they could have gone to Mr. Hardweil of the Railway Commission, men who are the equal in my judgment of any man they can import from the United States. I am sure the Canadian Pacific railway would have confidence in whatever opinion was given by Mr. Tiffin, and there are others on the Intercolonial whose evidence would be of material assistance if required. This evidence could he obtained within twenty-four hours. What good is a traffic expert from the United States who has not a knowledge of the conditions that prevail in railway operation in Canada. Our climatic conditions affect the road-bed and the rolling stock and the operation of trains, all of which are factors in the determination of the rates, and Canadian traffic experts are best qualified to give evidence on these points.

The hon. member for
Welland (Mr. German), speaking in this House on the 25th of April last said:
We have the Intercolonial. The best thing the Government of Canada could do for the people of Canada is to get rid of it at the earliest moment on the best terms it can possibly secure.
Does the hon. member for Westmorland agree with the hon. member for Welland in that?

In years gone by,
when the Hon. John Haggart, whose memory I revere, was a member of this House, he was talking the same thing with respect to the Intercolonial. I was no more responsible for his judgment in that respect than I am for the judgment of my hon. friend from Welland. My own opinion is known. I may say that when Mr. Hanna came before the Board of Railway Commissioners and said that if they lowered the rates there would be ruin and desolation to the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern, surely the onus was on him to prove it outside of his mere statement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is out of order, in the first place, because it refers to a debate which took place during the current session, and, in the second place, because it has no bearing on the subject under discussion.
The hon. gentleman introduced the question himself.
The hon. gentleman knows what my views are.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. members to the left of you are hardly sincere in this matter, judging from the remarks which they made on a previous occasion and the remarks which they have made during this debate. Some hon. members take the position that this Government are culpable for everything that may be a detriment to the

people in the West; whereas, if anything to the benefit of the West may emanate from this investigation, then the Railway Commission is to get credit for that benefit. It is manifestly unfair to take that attitude. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has taken the stand that the present Administration is not entitled to any credit for the investigation that is going on at present. He claims that this investigation is owing to a resolution that was introduced by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) some time last session. That resolution was introduced on the 25th of February; whereas I find the facts, so far as the beginning of this investigation is concerned, are that the hon. Minister of Railways when communicated with by the Board of Trade of Winnipeg submitted their resolution to the Railway Commission long before February. I wish again to read that letter addressed to the hon. Minister of Railways after he communicated that resolution to the Railway Commission. It is on record in 'Hansard,' vol. I, page 1930, and is as follows:
Ottawa, Nov. 24, 1911.
My dear Sir,-I beg to asknowledge receipt of yours of 20th inst., inclosing copy of resolution of the Winnipeg Board of Trade. This is the first complaint that has been directly made to the board regarding western rates generally. A good deal has appeared irom time to time in the western papers, but no step was taken by anybody there for a general investigation regarding rates throughout tneipro vinces of Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
No doubt you remember, Mr. Speaker, that during the discussion that took place on that occasion, the Prime Minister stated that so far as his Government was concerned he would see that there was a full investigation with regard to this matter and that counsel wTould be furnished in order that the public interest would be protected. This Government therefore took active measures to have this investigation take place as early as the 20th of November; 19JF whereas during all the years that the Opposition were in power they remained passive. It is true that an odd member here and there may have discussed this matter, but he never took an active interest on the floor of Parliament in order to press the Government which he was supporting to take action. When this resolution wrs brought up by the Opposition on the 25th of February, 1912, some months after the present Administration had taken active measures in connection with this investigation, they endeavoured to get some credit for the benefit that would result from that investigation. The attitude to-day is exactly in accordance with that line of policy. They to-day say: Do not make political
capital out of this matter, it is too important. But they are the ones who are endeavouring to make political capital out of it. They see the. benefit that is going to accrue to the West by this investigation, and they are endeavouring to slip in now and to make the cry that there is undue delay and to show to the public that they are the people who are forcing this investigation. The very remarks that have dropped from the lips of some of the speakers on the Opposition show this.
This is a very important question so far as the West is concerned. The Opposition members, instead of taking their present attitude, should endeavour to deal with this matter from a purely national standpoint and to do everything they can to assist the Government in bringing this investigation to a successful issue. Gentlemen, who have spoken on this matter from the left of Mr. Speaker, have endeavoured to make out that there should be absolutely no credit to the present Administration for the results or findings of the commission. It is true that great credit is due to the commission for what they have done. Owing to the large amount of business that necessarily comes before the commission it is not likely_ that they will take up big questions of this character on their own initiative unless they get assistance from the Government of the day. As the former Administration remained passive in this matter, the commission although charged with the same powers during the years that the [DOT]former Administration held office, did not exercise those powers until the present Government came into power. The people in the West will be right when they come to-the conclusion that they will expect some results out of this investigation. I am glad to see that the members on the Opposition benches are apparently sharing that view with the people of the West and are endeavouring to -claim some credit for the resuits that are going to accrue from this investigation, because we are satisfied that there will be some benefits to the people of the West when the commission have completed their duty. We see already the results with regard to express rates. Some years ago there was an investigation in connection with express rates, but we did not receive any benefits from it because the tormer Administration did not give that assistance to the commission which they should have given. In conclusion, I sub-JW1 j ,a^ the present Government is entitled to some credit for the manner in which they have dealt with this matter. Motion negatived.
