On motion of the Hon. Robert Rogers (Minister of Public Works), House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved that it is expedient (a) to provide for the incorporation of the National Gallery of Canada, and to transfer its property to and vest it in a board of trustees for the Government of Canada; (b) to authorize the board to acquire pictures, statuary, works of art and other property; and (c) to provide for the remuneration of such officers and servants as may be required, and for the reasonable travelling and other expenses of the board.
(Mt. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

The minister might
please explain the object of this resolution.

The object of the resolution is to provide that in place of managing our National Art Gallery by an advisory council, as in the past, it shall hereafter be managed under a board of trustees.
The National Art Gallery of Canada was the outcome of the establishment of the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts 1880, by the" Marquis of Lome, and Her Royal Highness the Princess Louise, during the term of their Vice-Royalty. This establishment placed in the hands of the hon. the Minister of Public Works, for public exhibition the diploma pictures which the newly appointed Academicians deposited on their election. From this beginning the national gallery has grown by means of the annual grants voted by the Dominion Government for the purpose. In 1907, the expenditure of these grants was placed in the hands of the Advisory Arts Council, whose first president was the late Hon. George Alexander Drummond, K.C.C.V.O., and whose members now are Sir Edmund Walker, K.C.M. G., C.V.O., L.L.D., D.C.L., president; Senator Arthur Boyer, and Dr. Francis J. Shepherd, while the work of the gallery is carried on by the director.
It will thus be seen that although the national gallery has been in existence for thirty-two years it has had only a very few years of systematic government, and during these last years such real progress has been made that it is possible to forecast a future for the national gallery of Canada which will see it take a fitting place among the art galleries of the British overseas dominions. The national gallery has now in its possession some four hundred paintings, drawings, etchings, and pieces of sculpture, and in addition an exceptionally well mounted and arranged collection of casts. This collection, which occupies the two lower floors of the space, allotted to the national gallery in the Victoria Memor-
Mr. McKAY.
ial Museum at Ottawa, takes up the story of sculpture at the Temple of the Parthenon, 447 B.C., carries it down through the great Hellenistic and Graeco_ Roman, periods to the Mediaeval Gothic of the eleventh and thirteenth centuries, and thence to the Italian and French Renaissance, leaving it for the present with the French portraits of the eighteenth century. In this exhibit, which is to be largely augmented, each object is prepared and coloured as nearly like its original as possible, and it is intended both for the visitor who comes for pleasure, and for the student who comes to copy, that it will prove a valuable opportunity to learn something of the history and progress of sculpture and design.
There is no doubt that Canada has, growing along with her material prosperity a strong and virile art which only needs to be fostered and encouraged in order to become a great factor in her growth as a nation. No country can be a great nation until it has a great art. I would like, however, since there seems to be some doubt about the matter, to make clear that this encouragement of our national art in its broadest and best sense is not achieved by the exclusive purchase of Canadian works of art. The purpose of the National Art Gallery is mainly educative, and as a knowledge and understanding of art is only to be gained by the comparison of one work of art with another, so for this comparison to lead always to higher ideals and understanding we needs must have in addition to our own Canadian pictures the best examples we can afford of the world's artistic achievements by which we may judge the merit and progress of our own efforts. It is on these lines that the purchase of works of art for the National Art Gallery is proceeding.
With this idea in view, it is believed that the art gallery can be best cared for bv handing it over to a board of trustees who will give it efficient and proper management, so that it will be conducted along lines that will carry out the views set forth in the memorandum I have just read.

I scarcely think the
committee will agree that the Minister of Public Works has afforded any reason why this resolution should be adopted. The plan which has been pursued in the past has been to leave the matter of the purchase of works of art and the calling for tenders for the various statues erected in public places, to the Advisory Art Council; this was done in connection with the erection of the statue on the St. Lawrence, and, indeed, everything connected with the art gallery. The Government has in the past been exceedingly fortunate in securing without remuneration the ser-

vinces of gentlemen who are thoroughly qualified to discharge these important duties. I can, therefore, see no reason why an incorporated body to be known as the Board of Trustees of the National Gallery of Canada should be appointed. I think it is upon my hon. friend to show some reason for making the proposed change. Is there any dissatisfaction with the present plan? Does it not work satisfactorily ? Does not the memorandum that the minister has read show that under the guiding hand of the Advisory Art Council during the years subsequent to the establishment of the gallery a very satisfactory advancement has been made, so that today the art gallery has become well worthy of Canada? There is another objection to the resolution, a portion of which reads as follows:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide for the incorporation of the National Art Gallery of Canada.
Is it intended to incorporate the National Art Gallery? Surely the intention must be to incorporate a board of trustees of the National Art Gallery of Canada. Someone has drawn the resolution, it seems to me without a proper appreciation of what should be done and what is intended to be effected. It would be absurd to incorporate the National Art Gallery, which consists of the pictures, exhibits, &c., and the rooms m which the works of art are kept, yet it is provided to incorporate the National Art Gallery and' to transfer its property to and vest it in a board of trustees for the Government of Canada. I think the hon. minister ought to explain what that means. It must be intended by this resolution to incorporate a board of trustees of the National Art Gallery of Canada, and transfer the property of the Government-the property which the Government now has in the various works of art-to this board of trustees proposed to be incorporated. The resolution goes on to say:
To authorize the board to acquire pictures, statuary, works of art and other property.
In the past the Minister of Public Works has authorized the advisory arts council to purchase only such works of art as have been provided for by Parliament by appropriations from year to year. Is it intended to change this procedure? Is it intended to vest in the board of trustees an arbitrary power to purchase such works of art as they see fit, and to commit Parliament from year to year to the payment of such bills as they may incur? If so, it is a very unwise power to give them. It seems to me that the resolution ought to be amended fb read:
To authorize the board, to the extent to which appropriations for the purpose may be
made from year to year by Parliament, to acquire pictures, statuary, works of art and other property.
While I was minister I declined to give the advisory art council any such arbitrary power as would seem to be embodied in this resolution; I asked Parliament each year for an appropriation, the amount of which was, I think, $10,000. The resolution goes on to say:
To provide for the remuneration of such officers and servants as may be required, and for the reasonable travelling and other expenses of the board.
I think that also should be provided by an appropriation from year to year. I cannot see the object of passing a resolution in these general terms, which, as I have said, would authorize this board to commit the country to a very much larger expenditure than Parliament might be willing to incur if it were called upon to vote the money from year to year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It seems to me to be somewhat incongruous that an art gallery should be under the control of the Minister of Public Works. The Minister of Public Works in Canada has to deal with the construction of breakwaters, the improvement of harbours, the erection of public buildings, and matters of that nature, which have to do entirely with the material advancement of the country. The man who is selected for the position of Minister of Public Works is chosen because he possesses qualities enabling him to deal with such matters to the advantage of the country and in the public interest. A man might be admirably adapted to the position of Minister of Public Works and for the carrying on of such matters of importance as would come before that department, and yet have very little of the training, culture or knowledge that would enable him to be a good judge of paintings, sculpture, and works of art, or to be in a position to know what should be selected in order to cultivate the artistic tastes of the people of the country. That has been recognized in the past by the appointment of this advisory committee. If the Minister of Public Works were selecting pictures or other works of art for the National Art Gallery, he would feel that he should be guided altogether by the advice of this advisory committee. That, at least, is the way I would feel, realizing that my knowledge of art was not sufficient to enable me to judge as to what should be purchased foT an art gallery; I would place the matter largely in the hands of this advisory committee. That plan, however, has not worked out satisfactory, and it is felt that it would be very much better to incorporate a body composed of men of taste and of talent, similar to those who have constitu-

ted the advisory committee in the past, and let them manage the art gallery, without the interference of the Minister of Public Works, and without calling upon him to confirm their judgment in regard to the works of art that time from time they might think it desirable to purchase. A somewhat analagous case occurred last year with respect to the Biological Board. That Board is composed of scientific men, chiefly representatives of the universities of the country and to facilitate their work I asked Parliament to establish the Biological Board, on a basis which would enable them to carry on their work unhampered by the Marine and Fishery Department. Parliament agreed and the Bill became law. It is not intended to give to this Board of Trustees a free hand to purchase whatever they please, irrespective of cost. But if we had a Minister of Public Works who would arbitrarily exercise his own judgment and overrule that of the advisory committee and of the trustees we might have a selection of works of art of an inferior quality which, instead of being a credit and ornament to the capital would be almost a disgrace.

Under this resolution
surely all that Parliament will have to do would be to foot the Bills.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend is criticising the framing of the resolution. The details of the measure will be in the Bill and I think he will find there that the points he has in mind are fully met.
This is a money Bill and the Bill cannot go beyond the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Bill will not go as far as the resolution.
The resolution should be in the same form as the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think it is clear what the meaning is and it would be hardly worth while to amend the resolution now.
It might be done in the committee now by unanimous consent.
Why not insert the words before National Gallery ' a Board of Trustees? '

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We might amend it to read:
That it is expedient to provide for the incorporation of a Board of Trustees of the National Gallery of Canada and to transfer the property in the said gallery to and vest it in the said board of Trustees for the Government of Canada.

I would suggest that, in order to make it clear, we should make a further amendment. We know very well that Boards of Trustees, if Mr. HAZEN.
given a free hand to acquire valuable works of art are very apt to use their judgment and to think that the Government will approve afterwards of what they do.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The only funds the Board can expend are those appropriated by Parliament and any funds they may receive by request or in any other manner and their expenditures are subject to review by the Auditor General.

Should there not be an appropriation which will govern them? It seems to me the Board ought always to have in view the appropriation which would be made. During the present session, for instance, the appropriation may not be made till the very last days of Parliament. They ought always to be kept within the appropriation.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not see how the money could be paid otherwise, the Auditor Gem eral would not sanction it.

Suppose they bought a picture in England for $20,000. It would be sent out here to the board. The statute authorizes them to buy it, and the Government is bound to pay for it. The Government would have to submit to Parliament a [DOT]vote for the purpose, otherwise a suit could be brought against the board and recovery made. There would be no escape for the Government, so far as payment is concerned. Why not s.iy:
, To authorize the .board to the amount of appropriations which may from time to time be made by Parliament to acquire pictures, statuary, works of art and other property.
Or:
To acquire pictures, statuary, works of art and other property to the amount of such appropriations as may from time to time be made by Parliament.
That would make it clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That would not be sufficient, because it is among the possibilities that people interested in work of this sort might make a bequest to the trustees for the purpose of buying pictures and works of art.
They could expend that outside of the statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
But you are limiting it.
The Bill puts it very plainly. In Bills introduced by means of a resolution, because they are money Bills, it is not usual to set forth all the details in the resolution. Section (b) of the resolution-
To authorize the board to acquire pictures, statuary, works of art and other property makes reasonably clear the intention of the Bill.	'

-does not give the trustees the slightest authority. The authority given to the trustees is given to them by the statute, and when the clause relating to that comes before Parliament it will be time to consider it. It seems to me that section (b) is. sufficiently c'ear so far as the resolution is concerned.

I do not wish to offer any serious opposition to this resolution, I merely wish to draw attention to the fact that it is another departure on the part of this Government from the principle of government and parliamentary responsibility. It is in the same class as the Bill in aid of agriculture, which removed to a large extent and for a term of years the responsibility from Parliament. This resolution proposes that a board shall be created to which money shall be voted, and that that board shall account to the Auditor General, but not to the Ministry or to Parliament. I admit it is not a very serious matter, but it is a principle to which I wish to register my objection. I do not think that the reasons so well given by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries are sufficiently weighty to warrant the important change in principle that is involved in this resolution. My hon. friend made a remark as to the unlikelihood of the Minister of Public Works being a competent art critic. Of course, while we will admit that an hon. gentleman may be a very excellent Minister of Public Works and not a capable art critic, there is no reason why a competent Minister of Public Works should not also be a competent art critic. I do not know that there is any reason for supposing that we have not at the present time in our present Minister of Public Works-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: You think he is an artist anyway.

-an hon. gentleman who would be entirely competent to discharge the duties and responsibilities that rest upon him in connection with the National Art Gallery. But even assuming that his recognized and universally known modesty would prevent him from assuming alone that responsibility, he has, as the Minister of Marine has said, the assistance of an advisory board, selected I presume by himself, or it may be by the Government, who may be the most competent and capable art critics that can be found. Possibly the men who are to-day the advisory hoard, would the the board contemplated under this resolution. There is no reason why competence shjuld not exist in the men who constitute an advisory board, as well as in a board who are to be given authority to expend public money outside the control of this Parliament. Even from the point of view which the Minister of Marine
and Fisheries has pi iced before the House,
I do not see any reason for making the change, and I see very great objection to the extension of the principle of expending public money without direct ministerial and parliamentary responsibility. It appears from this resolution, and from what has been said that >all Parliament has to do is to vote money from year to year and that the Auditor General will audit the accounts. That is not a satisfactory principle, and while this is not -a very important matter, and one in regard to which an exception would be permissible if in any, I submit that the principle is objectionable, and I do not think any sufficient reason has been advanced for departing from the principle which at present obtains.

I think my hon. friend
'will find when the Bill is introduced that every objection which has been raised is pretty well covered. When we get to the discussion of the Bill we shall be glad to consider any suggestion that hon. gentlemen opposite have to make. We are 'anxious to make the Bill as perfect as possible.

Is it the intention to
do away with the services of the present advisory board?
Not so far as I know.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They will be made the
trustees, I suppose?

I take it 'that when this Bill comes into effect there will be a committee-I do not know how many there will be on it, or (who will constitute it-to govern this National Gallery.
I have not travelled a great deal, but I have seen some art galleries open on Sundays, and I hope and trust that this committee when constituted will not be such strict Sunday observers as the present Min- * ister of Public Works and those who preceded him, but that they will insist on having the National Gallery open on Sundays. If a man goes into any art gallery in an American city, he sees a number of young women copying pictures. In that way a taste is cultivated, and these young women become artists good or bad. It seems to me tbat in a city like Ottawa, where there are so many people of different nationalities and of different religions, the National Art Gallery should not be closed on Sundays. I remember going down there one Sunday last winter, and to my amazement I found the place closed. I trust the committee when appointed will not take such strict Sabbatarian views as the Ministers of Public Works have taken in the past, but that they win be amenable to reason, will live in the light <af the present cen-
.SEVISED EDITION

fury, and will have the gallery open every Sunday in the year. The rich people have their automobiles and everything else, and why should it be denied to mechanics to take their children there on Sundays to see the works of art? Another matter which I think the advisory council should consider is that they should 'Sacrifice quantity Tather than quality.

The Minister of Public
Works has informed the committee that this resolution is to be the basis of a measure designed for the purpose of extending the scope of the Royal Victoria Museum as a Canadian national art gallery. If that idea is to be made effective, active efforts should be taken to procure art specimens from parts of Canada that have not hitherto been exploited. Up to the present, I think I am safe in saying, our art exhibits have been purchased from well known artists or from those whose repute has been personally known to the members of the committee entrusted with' their seleotion. I assume that I properly interpret the idea of a Canadian national gallery when I assert that the creations of Canadian artists should have a place there, whether they are to be found in marble palaces or in the humblest cottages of the land. Artists, like poets, are born, not made; Canada is a large country, and I am aware that there are specimens of art of a very high order to be found in places where art specimens have not hitherto been sought. I would hope that when this commission is appointed and the experts are to be sent abroad to gather Canadian art exhibits, a visit will be made by them to Nova Scotia and to the county of Richmond. There are in the village of Black River in the county of Richmond, specimens of the highest art, produced by ladies who were born in the county and whose works have received the highest encomiums when exhibited in the art galleries of Europe and of the United States. About 1845, two young ladies of culture and refinement, living in the old town of Arichat, and who were endowed with great artistic taste cultivated by study, undertook to produce certain historical pictures in embroidery, which they completed after fifteen years of most patient and exhaustive effort. These picture embroideries represent four historical events:	The
first is entitled, ' Concealment of the Regalia of Scotland, (1652).' This portrays an incident which occurred in Scotland at the time of the Commonwealth, when the regalia of Scotland were kept in Dunottar Castle. To prevent their confiscation during the siege *of the castle in 1652, they were cleverly conveyed away, through the midst of the unsuspecting besiegers, by Mrs. Grainger, the wife cf -the Minister of Kinneff Church, Mr. BENNETT (East Simcoe).
who took them to Kinneff, where they were safely buried near the pulpit by her husband. The second is an embroidery entitled ' Magna Charta,' which shows the barons of England demanding the charter from King John; there are twelve principal figures under the oak of Runnymede; the army is in the background. The third work is * David before Saul,' a scriptural picture, showing David playing the harp before Saul, and the Queen standing beside the latter. The fourth work is entitled ' Ossian,' and shows the poet Ossian when in hiding in the Highlands of Scotland; the fair Moira is kneeling beside him; the lake and snow-capped mountains are in the background. Each piece is almost four feet square and took four years to complete. Woven tapestries are quite common and are to be found in the art galleries of Europe and in many private residences in England and elsewhere, but this particular embroidered tapestry represented by these works of art is very rare indeed. There is only one similar specimen which I can recall and which was made by Fraulein Ripberger in Dresden, and which is now on exhibition in the art gallery in that famous city. It is a reproduction of Raphael's painting of the Sistine Madonna. The description of this work applies so particularly and minutely to the four pictures I am speaking of and which are the property of the lady in the county of Richmond, that I may be permitted to read it:
Famous painters have sought to copy Raphael's ' Sistine Madonna,' hut have laid their brushes down in despair.- And what painters have failed to do with the brush one woman has accomplished with her needle.
Fraulein Clara Ripberger, of Dresden, has dared to create-if is nothing less than a creation-this picture a second time. The bare suggestion of an embroidered copy of Raphael's masterpiece caused a smile when the exhibition of the Madonna in needle-work was announced in Dresden.
Curiosity alone drew an incredulous few to the first exhibition. But incredulity quickly turned to admiration. At the ordinary distance to a beholder the embroidery seemed a marvelously fine copy of the Madonna in oil. The spirit, the power of Raphael, seemed to have passed into the hand that did the work. The spell of the original was all there-the magnificence o,f the colouring, the expression of the faces, the- plasticity of the draperies, the haze of the cherubic glory and the sense of vision. Could this be embroidery?
Noted artists came and looked. They would not accept the word of the artist until they had examined both sides of the canvas and recognized that every square inch of the work was unmistakably done by the needle alone. The contention that the eyes at least had been painted had to be abandoned. Not a brushful of paint had touched the picture. Filoselle silk of various colours and in stitches of various lengths, had wrought the marvel. There was no suggestion of -tapestry

or Gobelin work. It is needle painting, not weaving, both in the flesh tones and expressions of the faces, and in the reproduction of the draperies.
I have stated that these ladies expended fifteen years in the work thus produced.	They sent to Europe for
the materials, and one can conceive the enormous amount of time and patience necessarily employed before the embroideries were completed. Industry and patience are often the accompaniments of great intellectual gifts and these gifts were possessed in a marvellous degree by the ladies I refer to. These were the Misses Elizabeth and Maria Ballam, daughters of a distinguished family in Richmond county seventy-five years ago. One of the ladies who assisted in this work died several years ago and the survivor has been totally blind for some time, so that it is not permitted to her in her declining years even to view the creations of her own artistic endowments. I have stated that these works were taken around the world and exhibited in various museums in Europe, Australia and the United States. A very large amount of money was offered for them by the late Senator Hearst of California in the year 1878, but the Misses Ballam thought that these pictures ought to be the property of the people of Canada and exhibited in some national museum here rather than become the property of a private individual in a foreign country. Inasmuch as the Minister of Public Works is now taking steps to further enlarge the purposes of the Canadian Art Gallery, I would suggest that he send one of his experts to Nova Scotia to make investigation as to the real artistic value of these embroideries. I do not asK him to purchase them unless they do possess real art value of which of course I have no doubt. I would suggest that after his commission is appointed and the experts employed, that no time should be lost in sending one of them to Richmond county to examine these works of art, lest they should fall into the hands of private owners. As I have said, the survivor of the ladies who produced these works is blind; she is eighty-two years old and has not long to live. She is willing that these pictures should become the property of the Canadian Art Gallery, and if the experts deem they are worthy of a place in the Royal Victoria Museum, efforts should be made by the minister and by his advisory board to acquire them for the nation.

I want to
say a word or two in support of the suggestion of my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte). I had the privilege some years ago of seeing the tapestries to which he refers. I am glad to know from his remarks that those tapestries are still in the possession of the Ballam family at Black River, and 285J
that it is possible that they may be had by the Government for exhibition in our national gallery. I have seen some tapestries in this country and in Europe; and while I do not pose as an art critic, I feel assured that if the board which we are about to create will send an expert down to examine those magnificent works of art, they will not be at all disappointed in the excellence of those tapestries. They are works of art and have been well preserved and have been exhibited in Europe, in the United States and in Australia. When the board is created, I hope that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) will make that suggestion to the chairman of that board, and have someone competent to judge as to the value of those works visit that farm House at Black River.
I am glad to say a word in support of this measure. In Canada we have been accused of the sin of materialism. In this age of materialism, we have been accused of being a most materialistic people, and I am glad to know that the aesthetic side of our nationality is being developed in this way, and I have no doubt that it will be more generously supported as art develops. I am glad to find that the pictures and statuary. that we have are so well housed in the museum. I feel, however, that the people of this city and country are not as well acquainted as they might be with the fact that we have an art gallery here. The incoming board might do very well in advertising those works of art which we have in the Victoria museum. I am glad to support the suggestion made by the hen. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) that for certain hours during every Sunday this gallery should be open to the public, and further, that during week days students should be permitted to enter that art gallery and to copy the pictures, and also that students of statuary should be able to go in there and to model as they do in every other art gallery of prominence throughout this continent and Europe. The primary idea in subsidizing an institution of this kind is to develop the love of art. I have no doubt, if this is done, the art gallery will serve a portion of our people and will take a place among our institutions that it has not taken in the past.

I wish to say a word
or two on this resolution, which I am pleased to endorse, although this seems to be a departure from the usual practice of keeping money under parliamentary control. We have seen what strides Canada has made during the past few years by the organization of the Department of Archives. Some years ago when the archives were lost, so to speak, in the Langevin block, the Hon. Mr. Fisher decided to appoint Dr. Doughty to erect a new building and to

give him a new staff, giving him at the same time large powers to acquire valuable papers. Dr. Doughty was in a position to organize a department which is certainly a credit to Canada, and I might say to North America itself. The most valuable collections are to be found in our Canadian archives. The same might also be said of this new art gallery which Canada now intends to have.
I second wdth pleasure the remarks which have been made by my hon. friend from Eichmond (Mr. Kyte). There are untold treasures in this country, not to speak of what my friend has mentioned as existing in the county of Eichmond, which according to his statement would be chefs-d'oeuvre. A few years ago an artist from England came to Canada, with the intention of spneding only a few weeks in Quebec. Whilst there he visited Laval University and a few of the oldest families. He discovered there some of the most remarkable paintings that exist in the world to-day. The result was such that he decided to stay in Canada; and, if I mistake not, he is still in the city of Quebec repairing and repainting those pictures, most valuable all of them, which were found in and around Quebec. He discovered some very valuable paintings especially in the old parishes, that had been brought over at the time of the French Bevolution by the priests who fled from France. The churches in our province are full of those chefs-d'oeuvre, and it might well occupy the time of our Art Commission to locate them.
My hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has spoken very strongly in favour of opening the museum on Sundays. I know that Canada is a very religious country, but I always thought that Sabbath observance was a special feature of the great city of London, England. If anyone of us goes to London, even in that stern and unbending Sunday observing city, one finds practically all the museums and all the art galleries open to the public on that day. I remember the last time I went to England-and the first time-to my surprise, I could visit these galleries. I spent one Sunday afternoon in the famous Wallace collection. If in London they are not scandalized at the idea, surely we in the city of Ottawa should imitate our kinsmen on the other side of the Atlantic.
Mr. Chairman, I take great pleasure in the fact that the people of this country are awakening to the beauties of art. Until some years ago the reproach which my hon. friend from the Yukon mentioned a moment ago, that we were a materialistic people was only too true. Perhaps there was not in the country the wealth there is today. Wealth has that special feature, that it brings forth the culture and the love of art. The death of Mr. Pierpont Morgan is probably tlie best example that wealth can bring Mr. LEMIEUX.
art to America and can be made the cause of splendid collections being acquired for the American people. Not very long ago, the millionaires-because there are now many millionaires in Montreal-started a gallery on Sherbrooke street and it is quite a credit to the city. I am told that at the last Salon some very beautiful paintings were exhibited there; and I understand that from year to year we are not only to have Canadian art productions but also the competition of foreign artists who will exhibit their paintings with those of Canadian artists. May I ask the Minister of Public Works if the old advisory board is to be maintained as part of the new corporation to be created by this Bill?

That is the intention, so
far as I know.

Because Sir Byron
Walker, Senator Boyer and Dr. Shepherd have given their time gratuitously for the cause of art, and they are men of high standing in the community, men of knowledge and of sterling honesty and even though there is a change of government, they should be maintained in the positions which they have occupied not for their own benefit, but for the benefit of the public, giving their services, as I have said, gratuitously. The Minister of Public Works says they will be maintained. For my part, I shall vote for the Bill with pleasure.

I have been communicated with by a few artists of prominence, one in particular, who protested against the manner in which the Canadian national gallery, has been collected in the past, and I must say that I agree with him. I am not an artist nor do I subscribe to the theory that if people want pictures they should paint them themselves. I am more broad-minded than that, but at the same time, I do insist that a national gallery should be national. Some mention has been made here of copies. It requires but little knowledge of art to know that in a matter of this kind copies of paintings do not count at all. They do little to develop originality. A national gallery which would warrant the expenditure of large sums of money- for you cannot get artistic productions for small sums-should be for the development of Canadian art, not only Canadian artists but Canadian subjects. We have in Canada not only magnificent opportunities but many artists of note and talent. Their achievements abroad have shown that. But I do think it is inexcusable that our national gallery should register a long list of paintings by foreign artists and on foreign subjects. If private collections are to be made of these things, that is all right, but sd far as I am concerned, I Mo not think the Government is warranted in developing

what may be called foreign art. It is too late to speak at length, but I enter my protest against the development of a Canadian national gallery on any other lines than these.
Resolution reported.
Mr. ROGERS thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 186, to incorporate the National Gallery of Canada.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
On motion of Mr. Rogers, House adjourned at 11.05 p.m.
